item.title: Grand Theft Auto: An American Icon, Born in Britain
item.description:
This America is wild and sexy, violent and vulgar. It’s a place for rebels, where freedom is not what the law allows, but what people can get away with before anyone can stop them.

Or, at least, that’s the America of Grand Theft Auto, the blockbuster franchise whose latest entry is releasing on Thursday as possibly the most anticipated video game ever. For many fans, the series may seem more American than apple pie.

But, like apple pie, this American icon originated in Britain and was made by people across the world, even as it has become a defining image of America itself for many players, shaped by movies, music and pop culture.

“It’s America as the rest of the world received it, through ‘Miami Vice,’ gangster rap, ‘Scarface,’ and MTV,” said Joost van Dreunen, a games professor at N.Y.U. Stern.

It’s a collage of familiar cultural exports, “which is exactly why it feels so familiar,” he added. “That’s the country America sent abroad.”

Grand Theft Auto did not start with Americans — or, at least, not all that many of them.

Instead, it was born and raised in Scotland and its first entry was released in 1997, after its creators intentionally stoked a British media frenzy about its scandalous vulgarity.

It worked. Sales soared. Sequels abounded. Rockstar Games, the studio that now develops the franchise, has sold hundreds of millions of copies and made enormous profits.

The new game, Grand Theft Auto VI, has already surpassed 15 million pre-orders, according to data tracker Sensor Tower. That represents $1.5 billion in revenue, so mammoth that some hope its success could revive the troubled game industry.

But in the early years, G.T.A.’s creators had only their imaginations — and the movies they watched and music they listened to — to build their world.

They didn’t have the budget to do much of anything else, Paul Farley, one of its designers, told The Guardian in a 2015 interview: “There were no fact-finding trips to the U.S.”

That, video game experts said, is part of why the America in Grand Theft Auto is so uncanny, and so successful.

Grand Theft Auto is like “an image of America’s image of itself,” said William Huber, a professor of game studies at Falmouth University in England.

“It’s an image that America has been exporting to the rest of the world for well over a century, and G.T.A. reflects an exaggerated version of the image,” he continued. “Americans find it recognizable, because they’re seeing their own media, with the volume turned to eleven.”

Its settings are not 1:1 replicas of real cities. Instead, they are hyper-detailed simulations of cultural icons. The Liberty City of one game, for instance, has versions of many New York signatures, like Times Square, Central Park and Brighton Beach.

But the crime and violence — the police chases, helicopter heists and rocket launcher attacks — are the stuff of extravagant Hollywood excess. This is a game built on the music and films and music videos that America sent out into the world in the 1980s, ‘90s and 2000s.

As a Frankenstein’s monster of pop culture, the games have had extraordinary results. They scandalized some with their sex and violence, delighted many with their chaos, provided a stage for Shakespeare and even kicked off discussions about the artistic simulacra of Borges and Baudrillard.

“We can see a lot of how the world imagines the U.S. in G.T.A.,” said Carly Kocurek, a historian at Illinois Institute of Technology who studies new media and video gaming. “It’s not a particularly flattering portrait.”

Rockstar has studios worldwide, including in New York and Los Angeles, and Americans were deeply involved in the games’ development — tailoring their virtual cities to those outside their windows.

But for players in many countries, the series may offer the most immersive “America” they ever experience. The studio’s games have largely taken place in fictional versions of New York, Los Angeles and Miami — Liberty City, Los Santos and Vice City in the games. (Plus towns and territories of the American West and South in the studio’s Red Dead Redemption games.)

Rockstar developers are famous in the industry for their assiduous attention to little things: thousands of distinct and carefully tailored characters, mantle decorations in homes, stocks on store shelves and more.

So for many international players, the American cities of G.T.A. may be more influential than ever because they “are the first North American cities they ever ‘lived’ in,” said Professor Huber.

But Rockstar is also known for its acidic satires of American culture, sometimes imbued at the tiniest level. There are in-game radio stations and TV shows, video games within the video game. Stephen Totilo, a veteran video game reporter who publishes the Game File newsletter, described one in-game show as “the adventures of xenophobic warrior astronauts who don’t worry much about collateral damage.”

“The games have never been reverent about the U.S.,” he added.

The G.T.A. games offer a biting critique of U.S. culture, said Patrick Prax, a professor in the game design department at Uppsala University in Sweden.

“The players, on the one hand, enjoy the freedom of this neoliberal fantasy — of ‘I can do anything,’” he said.

But that outlaw fantasy is twisted, he added: “It’s a cynical engagement with the myth of the ‘free America.’”

That has always been the games’ way, even when global opinion of the United States was high. Since the last game’s release 13 years ago, though, the country’s standing has fallen among many people around the world; the Pew Research Center found this year that more countries felt positively about China than America.

But experts said the G.T.A. series has grown into more than a reflection of how the world imagines America — at this point, the games are so big they also shape how people see the country. And, Professor Huber said, that imagined America is still obviously attractive.

“The year’s biggest cultural event will be millions of people around the world choosing to spend weeks inside an American city,” he said. “The world can lose faith in Washington and still want to live in Vice City.”

item.title: Isolated Amazon Indigenous Group Makes Rare Contact
item.description:
Community members in a Brazilian village in the Amazon rainforest were astonished this week to see a group of isolated Indigenous people emerge from the brush and ask for food, government officials said.

On Monday morning, a group of Indigenous Awá people made rare contact with the villagers, according to a statement from Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples. The encounter raised fears that decades of illicit deforestation, cattle ranching and hunting have pushed the forest’s inhabitants to a breaking point.

It was the first time in recent memory that a group of Awá had willingly left their isolated lives to make contact, said Sarah Shenker, a campaigner at the Indigenous rights group, Survivor International.

“They’ve shown so clearly for so long that they don’t want contact with outsiders,” said Ms. Shenker, who has visited the area regularly since 2010. “So this moment is really alarming.”

Videos and images of the Awá, taken by community members and shared by Survivor International, a U.K.-based group, show adults and children huddled near the edge of the forest in the northeastern Brazilian state of Maranhão. Some are bearing necklaces and headdresses, or holding spears. In all, they numbered around 20, the right group said.

The Awá initially approached nearby officers from FUNAI, a government agency that supports Indigenous communities, officials said.

Communicating through gestures, the Awá asked for yams, which they brought back into the forest, Ms. Shenker said. Some members of the Awá group continued to come and go in the following days, she said.

The immediate concern was for their health, Ms. Shenker said.

Lacking both exposure to common pathogens and vaccinations, Ms. Shenker said, the Awá were vulnerable to any diseases they might catch from the Guajajara. That is a larger group of Indigenous people in Maranhão.

As images and videos of the encounter began to circulate on social media, Brazil’s Indigenous peoples ministry mobilized a response involving local and national health authorities.

“Brazilian policy for the protection of isolated Indigenous peoples is guided by the principle of non-contact,” the statement said. “Its objective is not to promote relations with these peoples, but to guarantee the necessary conditions for them to remain in isolation if that is their decision, without external interference and with full protection of their territories.”

For decades, wildfires, illicit logging, ranching and hunting have led to the destruction of Indigenous peoples’ livelihoods in the Amazon, Ms. Shenker said. The government has designated certain areas as protected Indigenous land, she said, but now, “this territory and a few other Indigenous territories in the region are the only places where valuable hardwoods still stand.”

About 15 years ago, the Guajajara people formed groups called the “Forest Guardians,” which confronted illegal logging camps and confiscated equipment, Ms. Shenker said at least six of them were killed while doing so, she said.

While some Awá people have chosen to make contact, Ms. Shenker said, about three or four subgroups reject contact with outsiders. The Awá move freely and survive entirely from the forest, she said, hunting wild boar, deer, monkeys and fish and gathering fruit and honey. They build shelters from tree fibers.

The forest is also their source of medicine and spirituality, she said.

Survivor International has not yet reached any conclusions about why the Awá emerged this week, but said it was troubling.

“The fact that they’ve come out now does indicate that they have probably felt forced to for one reason or another,” Ms. Shenker said. “And as we say, because their lives are so intricately related to the forest, it would be impossible to completely separate the pressures on the land.”

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
President Trump is expected to sit down with Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in China on Thursday, concluding his whirlwind Asian trip with a three-way summit in which he may discuss nuclear weapons and the wars in Iran and Ukraine with the authoritarian leaders.

The meeting in the city of Shenzhen, a metropolis just north of Hong Kong, will be the first of its kind between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States. Officials who planned the trip have cautioned that they do not expect major breakthroughs or agreements. But that seems beside the point for the three men, who all seem intent on projecting their power.

Mr. Trump will also meet separately with both leaders in Shenzhen, which is hosting a summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, a group of 21 economies. As APEC leaders gathered on Thursday morning, Mr. Xi, Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin warmly shook hands with each other as they took their positions for a group photo before attending a meeting.

With Mr. Xi, Mr. Trump is seeking to reassert American leadership in artificial intelligence and to pin the Chinese leader down on extending a trade truce that is set to expire in January. The president also hopes to persuade Mr. Xi to continue to allow shipments of rare earths and magnets to the United States.

With Mr. Putin, the American president intends to discuss the war in Ukraine. He has not seen the Russian leader in person since August 2025, when Mr. Trump hosted him for a bilateral meeting in Alaska. Mr. Trump left the meeting with only a promise of a later agreement on the war that has not materialized.

Mr. Putin has been under increasing pressure to resolve the war in Ukraine, which has weakened his country’s economy and caused high Russian casualties. Still, he has shown little inclination to end the invasion, and is expected to keep fighting at least through the winter, according to Western intelligence assessments.

For his part, Mr. Xi may hope that the three-way meeting in China symbolizes a leveling of global power, a shift to a future where the United States is not the dominant player. He is expected to telegraph his close relationship with Mr. Putin while extending a flattering welcome to Mr. Trump, who is known to enjoy the ceremonial trappings of power. Mr. Xi also wants to show off the city of Shenzhen, a software and robotics hub.

On nuclear weapons, Mr. Trump is prepared to talk about Beijing’s growing arsenal with Mr. Xi, his advisers said, though it is a topic the Chinese are reluctant to discuss. China is on track to have 1,000 nuclear warheads by 2030, producing them at a pace that has worried U.S. officials and analysts.

Here’s what else to know:

A.I. race: Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump both spoke about A.I. in their remarks at the APEC meeting. The Chinese leader called on the group to build an “open ecosystem” for the technology, a notable comment given the competition for A.I. supremacy between his country and the United States. Mr. Trump said in his APEC speech that he opposed A.I. regulation that would stifle growth.

Song choice: World leaders were welcomed with fanfare by Chinese musicians at a banquet on Wednesday. For Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan, the band played a song inspired partly by postwar protests against the U.S. military presence in her country. Was it a message to a close American ally? Read more ›

Yalta’s shadow: It appears unlikely that the trilateral meeting will live up to the comparisons to the conference in Yalta, where Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met toward the end of World War II to divide up the globe. Read more ›

item.title: A Village Burned, Its People Killed or Exiled. Was It Genocide?
item.description:
As his village burned, Mustafa Kamal somehow kept his family safe.

Husband and wife, three sons, three daughters, a granddaughter, they ran until their breath ran out. They stumbled past bodies of people they knew, shot by Myanmar’s security forces. They slogged through mud that claimed some of their clothes and trekked over jungle passes thick with leeches. Days later, when they finally crossed a river into Bangladesh, they rowed past swollen bodies of other Rohingya Muslims who never made it to the other side alive.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice in The Hague is ruling whether the atrocities against the Rohingya ethnic minority constitute a genocide waged by the Myanmar state. The killing, gang rape and mass arson reached a furious zenith in 2017, building on years of systematic persecution. Three quarters of a million Rohingya flooded into Bangladesh in a matter of weeks, the most rapid refugee exodus in recent history. And more kept coming.

A judgment in a country half a world away would matter, Mr. Kamal told me. It would acknowledge the fate of his home, Zammona, one of 400 Rohingya villages that were obliterated by Myanmar security forces nine years ago.

But sitting in the dark, cramped shelter that is now his home in Bangladesh, part of what is now the world’s largest refugee settlement, Mr. Kamal said that the trauma did not end nine years ago. For the Rohingya, he said, misery never ends.

International aid to the camps has plummeted. Hunger and disease are rampant. In May, Mr. Kamal’s 18-year-old son was killed by Rohingya militants who have unleashed a reign of terror in the refugee camps. Human traffickers roam the narrow spaces between tarpaulin shelters, grabbing men, women and children. One of Mr. Kamal’s daughters was kidnapped by a militant, who forced himself on her. She had no choice but to marry him, and they now have a baby boy.

“Oh, Allah, why is there no justice for the Rohingya anywhere on earth?” Mr. Kamal said, weeping as he clutched a photo of his dead son.

Mr. Kamal, now 66, grew up in Zammona, a fertile collection of hamlets in Myanmar’s far west, dotted with fish ponds, well-stocked groceries and mosques with graceful arches. His father was a teacher at a government school. Mr. Kamal learned Burmese, the language of Myanmar’s Buddhist Bamar majority, and took a job as a trader, ferrying goods from one town to another. His wife, Toyuba Khatun, was educated, too.

The Rohingya had long faced repression from the military, which ruled Myanmar for decades and preserved power for the Bamar. In the 1980s, the Rohingya lost their legal status in Myanmar, their citizenship essentially stripped from them. Babies rarely were issued birth certificates. There was also occasional tension with the Rakhine ethnic group, with whom the Rohingya shared Rakhine State.

Still, Mr. Kamal said he had easy relations with Rakhine villagers who lived nearby. After all, he had gone to school with them; his father had been their teacher.

A store owner in Zammona, Mohammed Yunus said he welcomed Buddhist customers, bantering with them as they haggled over the latest clothes or electronics. (Zammona is called Zin Paing Nyar in the Burmese language.)

In 2012, violence flared between the Rohingya and the Rakhine, inflamed by state media coverage. Gatherings of more than five Rohingya were banned. Mosques were shuttered. Many Rohingya children no longer felt welcome at government schools. Mr. Kamal’s father secretly taught his grandchildren at home, desperate for the next generation to be educated.

When Mr. Kamal’s daughter Rehana Bibi got married, a Myanmar official forbade her from having more than two children. A false narrative took hold across Myanmar that the high birthrate of Rohingya was part of a global Muslim plot to swamp Buddhist lands. Military propaganda inaccurately portrayed the Rohingya as illegal immigrants from Bangladesh. Never mind that Rohingya had been elected to Parliament, studied at the nation’s finest universities, and once enjoyed government radio broadcasts in their own language, just like any other of the nation’s many ethnic groups. In the 2015 elections, which elevated the party of Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, the Nobel Peace laureate, the Rohingya lost their right to vote.

On Oct. 9, 2016, a militant group led by a Rohingya refugee who was born in Pakistan and schooled in Saudi Arabia launched attacks on Myanmar security outposts, killing nine police officers, according to the Myanmar authorities.

The security forces’ response to the attacks punished an entire ethnicity.

In Zammona, Mr. Kamal locked the door to his spacious wooden house and prayed with his family that the soldiers would not attack.

Over the next few months, soldiers rounded up men in Zammona, accusing them of participating in the militant raids, charges they denied. Their only crime, they said, was being young, able-bodied Rohingya men. One was given a 54-year prison sentence. Soyadul Amin and Abdul Rohim were sentenced to 16 years each. Mr. Amin described how the Myanmar soldiers tied his arms behind his back, threw him on the ground and laughed as they ordered him to lap up his food like an animal. When he and others cried out for water, the soldiers offered urine.

The United Nations said at the time that hundreds of Rohingya were killed and that the crackdown “very likely” constituted crimes against humanity.

“We could not imagine what would happen next,” Mr. Kamal said. “Our people, our Rohingya were finished.”

On Aug. 25, 2017, the Rohingya militants carried out another series of attacks, killing more than a dozen security forces. This time, the military was prepared. Within hours, the scorched-earth retribution began.

Mr. Kamal heard the rocket launchers crescendo from the east. He gathered his family, but there was no time to grab anything, apart from a few precious papers that proved their existence in Myanmar.

Mr. Yunus, the store owner, marshaled his kin. As he left his two-story home, with its spacious garden and surrounding fields, he made sure to lock the door. He would surely be back, he thought.

“I was a rich man in Myanmar,” he said. “I had everything I needed for my family.”

As the soldiers descended on Zammona, Fatema Khatun, the wife of Mr. Amin, one of the men sent to prison, searched frantically for her seven children and thanked Allah that they were all there. She was seven months pregnant with her eighth child. Along their long escape to Bangladesh, a Myanmar soldier grabbed one of her daughters, Sukura Begum, in the forest and raped her, just one horror in what U.N. investigators say was systematized sexual violence. She was 11 years old.

Elsewhere in the village, Morijan, a young mother who goes by one name, searched for her 9-year-old son, Mohammed Omair, who had raced to the west when the artillery began. Two days later, he was found in a rice paddy with a bullet wound through his heart.

At least 10,000 Rohingya were killed by security forces and Rakhine mobs in the immediate aftermath of the 2017 attacks, the U.N. estimated. In Zammona, 10 unarmed men were trussed and killed, then tossed in a mass grave north of the village, said a Myanmar soldier whose testimony, after he ended up in the hands of an enemy militia, marked the first time perpetrators confessed to their crimes. The soldier also said seven Rohingya were shot dead there.

Zammona was wiped from the map, its ruins smoldering for days, visible from a hill in Bangladesh. When he was released from a Myanmar prison four years later, his 16-year sentence commuted, Mr. Rohim returned home before he, too, fled across the border.

“Everything was gone,” he said of Zammona. “I couldn’t recognize anything.”

The Myanmar government soon covered up evidence of the village, building rows of prefab housing on burned earth.

All that was left of Zammona was a large Bodhi tree, sacred to Buddhists because it was the kind under which a prince meditated and gained enlightenment as the Buddha.

In Bangladesh, Mr. Kamal and his family were allotted a tiny shelter with a tarpaulin cover. They could not leave the refugee camps without permission. International assistance allotted each person $12 a month for food, decreased now to $10.

Fatema Khatun’s daughter, who was raped, suffers from debilitating seizures. Three years ago, another daughter, then 18, disappeared for months, then called tearfully from Malaysia, where she said she had been trafficked. She was forced to marry an older man, she said, 50 or 60 years old, she wasn’t sure.

Five years ago, Ms. Khatun’s husband, Mr. Amin, was released from prison a broken man. His kidneys barely work from the beatings. He lies on the floor of their shelter, groaning from an ache that never dissipates. There is no money for painkillers. Occasionally, he repeats the Burmese words he learned in detention: a string of numbers that was his prisoner ID.

“I was supposed to die,” he whispered. “I don’t feel alive.”

On Monday, children crammed into Mr. Kamal’s shelter. His 10-year-old grandson recounted how the boy had been held by the militants, his hands reaching wide to show the size of the blades they brandished. One granddaughter was quiet, but over the hours she leaned against me. Later, she offered a tentative “hello” in English. We practiced sentences.

What is your name? Sadeka Bibi.

How old are you? 13.

Where are you from? Her English faltered. The answer came translated as the block number of her refugee camp. Her mother intervened. Sadeka tried again.

“I am Rohingya,” she said. “I am from Myanmar.”

Mohammed Faisal Arakani contributed reporting.

item.title: After Train Crash, Spain Asks if High-Speed Rail Grew Too Fast
item.description:
Spain is in the middle of a growth spurt. Immigrants are driving the population to a record high of nearly 50 million. Tourism has skyrocketed and is set to attract nearly 100 million people, 25 million more than in 2016. With one of Europe’s fastest-growing economies, Spain has invested tens of billions of euros in digitalization and renewable energy.

But a horrific train crash that killed 69 people last month, only nine months after a collision on the same high-speed line killed scores more, has raised concerns about the state of Spanish civil infrastructure. It has also left Spaniards asking if their country has grown too fast for its own good.

With national elections set for this month, infrastructure has moved from esoteric policy papers to the campaign trail.

Opposition politicians say the left-wing government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has let the country go to seed. Some experts argue that his government was overly focused on new investments instead of maintaining old ones like roads, water systems and the high-speed rail network, the world’s second-largest, behind China’s. One think tank found that spending per high-speed rail passenger fell by more than a quarter in the decade leading to 2024.

“The system is under strain,” said Pere Navarro, the Spanish civil servant responsible for highway traffic. Spain’s infrastructure and public services, he said, were designed for “when there were 40 million of us” but now “we have a population of 50 million and welcome 100 million tourists every year.”

Mr. Sánchez’ government said that, though Spain needed to increase investment in its railways, it was the center-right former government that led the country until eight years ago that had eroded infrastructure, and especially railway infrastructure, with years of austerity policies.

Mr. Sánchez, pressed on the lack of maintenance in a television interview on Wednesday, argued that his government had worked to “reverse the cuts to the railway system” by his conservative predecessor. He also promised the equivalent of an additional $21 billion on maintenance and safety spending through 2030.

Much of Spain’s infrastructure dates to a previous boom era, soon after the country joined a precursor to the European Union in 1986. Suddenly awash in the bloc’s funds, it spent the 1990s revamping its industrial capitals, like Barcelona and Bilbao, and building a sprawling high-speed rail system and broader highways.

By the early 2000s, as Spain kept spending billions on transit infrastructure, it gained global renown for its high-capacity rails and roads. But a series of setbacks hit the country hard. Investment in infrastructure fell off after the financial crisis in 2008 and the popping of Spain’s housing bubble.

As Spain became wealthier and E.U. priorities shifted east, European funds dried up. Then, after the 2008 financial crash, Europe’s sovereign debt crisis nearly halved public investment in Spain, once higher than the European average. The spending didn’t recover under either right- or left-leaning governments. Now, Spain is spending, in real terms, about 25 percent less on infrastructure than it did in 2000, according to the Valencian Institute of Economic Research.

In 2018, Mr. Sánchez, of the Socialist Party, took office. After managing Spain through the coronavirus pandemic, he used a round of enormous E.U. recovery funds to focus on growth.

“Spain is in fashion,” Mr. Sanchez said at a tourism fair last year.

In a sign of his confidence in Spanish rail infrastructure, his government proposed banning short flights to cut carbon emissions. He used increased tax revenues from an influx of immigrant workers to fill the government coffers and offer popular subsidies and social benefits.

As the country’s gross domestic product soared, its investment in infrastructure didn’t keep pace. Last year, a national blackout exposed the weaknesses of the country’s saturated energy grid. It depends increasingly on the renewable sources that Mr. Sánchez’ government has prioritized, a factor that experts have said may have made it less stable. Analysts and energy companies also say the grid’s limitations make it harder to supply electricity to new construction projects, slowing building projects and contributing to a housing shortage. Protests over housing and high rents this year prompted Mr. Sánchez to call for early elections.

The blackout inspired a book by the economic think tank Funcas that argued that “political considerations influencing decisions” contributed to obsolescence and breakdowns of Spain’s transport infrastructure, water networks and energy assets. The authors said that the government should instead “prioritize maintaining existing infrastructure over new investment.”

They weren’t alone.

“In Spain, many things that once worked well now work poorly,” Ramón González Férriz, a political analyst, wrote in a much-discussed article in El Confidencial, a center-right news outlet, after the recent train crash. He blamed the government for prioritizing benefits and subsidies over maintaining public works that, he wrote, “take a long time to bear fruit and may go unnoticed by voters.”

The government’s initial response to the crash was not to focus on maintenance flaws but to blame the human error — revealed in leaked audio from a train traffic control center — in which a controller directed one high-speed train into a stalled train on the same track. But the second deadly crash in a year prompted inevitable questions about railway infrastructure and safety.

The transportation minister, Óscar Puente, who subsequently resigned, lamented that because the government did not control a majority of lawmakers in Parliament, it could not pass a budget that invested more in railway maintenance. Since then, Mr. Sánchez has responded to criticism with a mix of blame for conservative predecessors, defense of his government’s spending level and promises to increase it.

Conservative opponents, including from the Popular Party, which leads election polls, say Mr. Sánchez has full responsibility for any infrastructure shortcomings after eight years in power.

Spain is suffering from “continued negligence” under Mr. Sánchez that has put Spaniards at risk, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the Popular Party leader, said this month.

Train usage in Spain has risen drastically since 2021, when Mr. Sánchez’ government opened the country’s market for high-speed passenger trains to competitors. Ticket prices fell by more than 40 percent, and hundreds of miles of new high-speed rail routes were opened. Last year, 44.5 million passengers used high-speed rail, twice as many as in 2019.

But according to the Institute of Economic Studies, a Madrid think tank associated with Spain’s largest association of employers, maintenance spending per high-speed passenger dropped 27.5 percent between 2015 and 2024. At the time of the accident, Spain was among the European countries that spent the least on maintaining its rail network.

Spain’s passengers had begun to notice delays, with on-time arrivals dropping nearly 10 points to roughly 86 percent in 2024, according to Spain’s competition regulator.

Train drivers warned last year of track deterioration on the high-speed route to Seville, the line where the crashes occurred.

Beyond the issue of high-speed rail maintenance, transportation experts have said that Spain’s entire strategy of prioritizing high-speed rail makes little sense because over 80 percent of Spain’s passenger rail trips last year were on shorter-distance commuter lines that have suffered from years of neglect.

Spain’s Independent Authority for Fiscal Responsibility, an autonomous state-appointed body, reported that between 1990 and 2018, Spain invested 15 times more on high-speed rail than on commuter rail, a trend that continued under Mr. Sánchez.

But Mr. Sánchez’ focus on high-speed rail was not just a government priority. Mr. Puente, the former transportation minister, pointed out at the time that regional politicians all over the country had demanded high-speed rail, regardless of their political affiliation.

“Look at this country’s history over the past 20 or 30 years,” he said. “If you don’t have high-speed rail, you’re nobody.”

item.title: Headquarters of Saudi Sovereign Fund Damaged as Houthis Attack Riyadh
item.description:
A skyscraper housing the offices of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund was damaged during an apparent Houthi missile attack on Thursday, underscoring the spiraling costs for the kingdom in its renewed war with the Iran-backed Yemeni militia.

A Times reporter who visited the city’s financial district in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, which is home to the skyscraper, the Public Investment Fund Tower, saw damage to the 80-story building. Black scorch marks were visible around the midsection, and windows on about five floors had been blown out.

Residents of Riyadh, heard a large explosion early Thursday. Soon after, the Saudi authorities reported an attempted Houthi missile attack and said that “falling shrapnel,” which typically results from a missile or drone interception, had caused damage in the city, without specifying where.

The Houthis did not immediately comment on the attack, but they have claimed responsibility for multiple strikes on Riyadh’s financial district in recent weeks, including one that damaged a tower belonging to the Saudi state oil company, Aramco. The Houthis typically say that their attacks are in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen.

Saudi Arabia’s roughly $900 billion sovereign wealth fund is the engine of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plans to overhaul the national economy and reduce dependence on oil. Underpinned by oil revenue, the fund manages high-profile investments around the world, including stakes in major American companies such as Uber and SpaceX, in addition to vast domestic investments in artificial intelligence, manufacturing, sports and entertainment.

The fund and its subsidiaries occupy a lot of the financial district’s real estate, and damaging the headquarters would be a symbolic win for the Houthis.

There was no indication that anyone had been injured in the attack, which happened before the working day had started. Many employees in the financial district have been working from home in recent weeks amid persistent Houthi attacks.

A spokesman for the Public Investment Fund did not respond to a request for comment.

Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who control much of northern Yemen, have been exchanging escalating attacks for weeks, including on energy facilities and airports. Analysts say that the war is likely to drag on for months. Abdulrahman al-Rashed, a Saudi commentator who is close to the kingdom’s leadership, said in a podcast interview last month that the conflict could last up to two years.

In Yemen, where the Houthis are engaged in heavy fighting with the Saudi-backed government, the impact has been devastating, exacerbating a dire humanitarian crisis. More than 2,200 people have been killed in the fighting over the past few months and nearly 350,000 displaced, according to the World Health Organization.

The two sides have been fighting on and off since 2015, after the Houthis took over the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, routing the internationally recognized Yemeni government and setting off a civil war.

Saudi Arabia led a disastrous bombing campaign to try to restore the Yemeni government to power, contributing to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people from violence, hunger and disease. A fragile truce took hold in 2022 but began to unravel in July amid the broader U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

A full-blown war erupted last month, when the Yemeni government declared a new military campaign against the Houthis, backed by Saudi warplanes.

So far, that campaign has made little headway, and analysts say the balance of power in Yemen continues to tilt toward the Houthis.

On Sunday, forces backed by Saudi Arabia in southern Yemen said that they were withdrawing from the Red Sea coast, where they have been fighting for weeks to retake strategic territory from the Houthis.

The following day, a royal order by Saudi Arabia replaced the general overseeing operations in Yemen, Fahd al-Salman, with General Fayyad al-Ruwaili, who is also chief of the general staff for the Saudi military.

For Saudi Arabia, the war has threatened to frustrate Prince Mohammed’s hopes of turning the country into a global hub for business and tourism.

A major attack on Riyadh’s airport last month killed at least 14 people and injured more than 300, forcing officials to shut down flights for weeks and cancel a series of high-profile events. Since then, near-daily Houthi attacks have disrupted life across the capital, a city of roughly eight million people.The building that was damaged on Thursday is the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh. It towers over the financial district, a development that also houses banks, multinational companies and luxury apartments.

The Public Investment Fund has played a major role in Prince Mohammed’s efforts to project influence abroad, though financial pressures have pushed Saudi officials to rein in some of their grandest plans.

On Thursday, a large area near the Riyadh tower had been cordoned off, and the neighborhood was mostly empty, save for a handful of security guards and other blue collar workers.

As a group of workers passed the damaged tower, they warned one another to keep their mobile phones in their pockets. The Saudi authorities have threatened to prosecute people who photograph or share information about attacks.

Saeed Al-Batati contributed reporting from Al Mukalla, Yemen.

item.title: Some leaders flew private to the APEC summit in Manila, but not Mexico’s president.
item.description:
Many of the world leaders who arrived in the Chinese city of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum traveled on private or presidential planes. President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico opted for a more low-key approach.

Ms. Sheinbaum arrived in Shenzhen by commercial flight, a grueling journey. On Saturday, she posted a video from Mexico City International Airport saying she would first fly to Tijuana and then on to Shenzhen. The three-hour domestic leg was followed by a flight to Shenzhen lasting roughly 15 hours.

The video showed her sitting in the terminal, greeting travelers and taking photos with fans at the boarding gate.

“It’s practically a two-day flight, and on top of that, there’s the time change,” she told EFE, the Spanish news agency.

After touching down in Shenzhen on Monday, Ms. Sheinbaum took a shuttle bus to a red carpet on the tarmac, where she was greeted by Chinese officials and dancers.

Chinese social media users praised Ms. Sheinbaum’s modest mode of travel as pragmatic. On Weibo, China’s version of X, posts about her arrival drew more than 10 million views.

It is not the first time Ms. Sheinbaum has flown commercial as president. She did the same for other major diplomatic trips — including the Group of 20 summit in Brazil in 2024 and the Group of 7 summit in Canada last year.

When she flew to Brazil commercially in 2024, her government said in a statement that it was in accordance with one of the principles of her government, which was austerity.

The practice of Mexican presidents traveling commercially began in December 2018 under Ms. Sheinbaum’s predecessor, Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who refused to board Mexico’s presidential jet upon taking office and left it parked for more than four years before selling it in 2023. He described the plane as an “insult to the people” and an example of excess, and vowed to forgo the luxuries often seen as political perks. He also said he would cut his salary, convert the sprawling presidential residence into an arts and culture center and dissolved the 8,000-member military presidential guard.

The Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner was ordered by former President Felipe Calderón and used by his successor, Enrique Peña Nieto. Mr. López Obrador spent several years struggling to find a buyer before selling the aircraft to Tajikistan for $92 million.

Jiawei Wang contributed reporting.

item.title: Greenland Pulls Closer to the U.S. — by an Hour
item.description:
For years, Jens Peter Lange has been annoyed about Greenland’s time zone. As a sometime fisherman and hunter in Ilulissat, a Greenlandic city above the Arctic Circle, it was simply disorienting.

“When we head out to go fishing, it’s dark. And when we come back, the sun is coming up,” he said. “It feels weird.”

So Mr. Lange and many other Greenlanders were pleased this month when Greenland’s government, after a heated discussion but an overwhelming vote in favor, decided to shift its time zone an hour earlier.

Greenland, an overseas territory of Denmark, is three hours ahead of Eastern Standard Time and three hours behind Central European Time, which Denmark uses. Starting next October, Greenland will move its clocks back one hour.

Even though closer ties to the United States were not part of the official reason for changing the time zone, and many Greenlanders remain upset about President Trump’s threats to “get” the island, the time shift could facilitate more opportunities for U.S. trade, tourism and investment in Greenland.

It also stands to distance the giant island from Denmark, which colonized Greenland more than 300 years ago and still oversees its defense and much of its foreign policy.

The time zone decision, made on Nov. 12, reverses what Greenland’s leaders did in 2023. Back then, they moved the clocks forward, striving to be closer to Denmark.

The idea was to facilitate more business and communication with Denmark and the rest of Europe. But the move prompted years of complaints, especially from hunters and fishermen who struggled with darker mornings.

And in recent years there has also been rising sentiment in favor of breaking from Denmark. Two opposition parties in Greenland’s Parliament that support fast-tracked independence spearheaded the vote.

Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland’s prime minister, who is relatively pro-Denmark, warned against turning the clocks back again.

He told parliamentarians that doing so would bring “a lasting negative economic impact on society as a whole, including public finances.”

He also said it could lead to fewer and more expensive flights because most come from Denmark, and create problems for Greenland’s health care services, which are heavily dependent on communication with Denmark.

Despite Mr. Nielsen’s warnings, the proposal passed easily, with support from his own party and no votes against it.

In the new time zone, Mr. Lange said, he will work better and sleep better.

“We will go back to our normal biological rhythm,” he said.

The tensions with Mr. Trump have eased since the United States signed a deal in September with Denmark and Greenland to expand the American military presence in Greenland.

But Mr. Trump’s fixation on the Arctic island has spawned a frenzy of American business people prowling for deals in minerals and natural resources. Some were excited by Greenland’s decision to shift time zones.

“I think it’s brilliant,” said Larry Swets, the executive chairman of Greenland Energy Company, a Nasdaq-listed corporation that does oil exploration. “Every extra hour Greenland and the U.S. share in the workday is an hour we can spend building something together.”

Thomas Dans, the chairman of the United States Arctic Research Commission and one of Mr. Trump’s most active allies on Greenland, said it would help facilitate U.S.-Greenlandic trade and tourism.

“The adjustment recognizes Greenland’s positioning within North America,” he said. “It’s a great move.”

item.title: Drone Hits Dutch Embassy Compound in Kyiv, Ukrainian Officials Say
item.description:
The Dutch Embassy in central Kyiv was damaged by a drone on Thursday, Ukrainian officials said, amid a wave of Russian attacks and threats of a dire response to Ukraine’s assault on the bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.

It was not immediately clear whether the embassy had been deliberately targeted, and other diplomatic facilities and embassies have been damaged in strikes over the course of the war. Still, the strike came a day after the Russian Embassy in the Netherlands condemned a Dutch defense company’s role in producing missiles used to hit the Kerch Strait Bridge, the Crimean bridge.

Tom Berendsen, the Dutch foreign minister, said a projectile had struck just behind the embassy compound, causing minor damage to the building.

“Fortunately, our colleagues are unharmed,” he said in a statement. “We are investigating exactly what happened.”

Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, urged world leaders “to condemn in the strongest terms Russia’s attacks on foreign diplomats.”

Russia’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately comment.

The blast near the embassy was one of many explosions across the Ukrainian capital on Thursday as Russia launched swarms of jet-powered drones at Kyiv, shortly after President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia vowed retaliation for the bridge attacks.

“There will be no negotiations, only retaliation,” Mr. Putin said in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, after meeting with President Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping. “Moscow’s response will be far more painful.”

Russia has already opened an intense bombing campaign against the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainians alive and functioning in the winter, launching daily waves of strikes that have especially targeted Kyiv and its energy system.

The Kremlin’s threats increased, though, amid Ukraine’s latest campaign to sever the Kerch Strait Bridge. That operation began on Monday, with waves of drones and missiles pounding the 12-mile crossing in a bid to sever a vital Russian military supply line.

Alongside domestically produced weapons, Ukrainian forces deployed a low-cost, jet-powered cruise missile made by Destinus, an aerospace and defense company headquartered in the Netherlands.

Destinus said after Tuesday’s strike that seven of its Ruta missiles had penetrated Russian air defenses, helping collapse a large section of the bridge into the sea.

item.title: In a Rohingya Refugee Camp, Jubilation but Also Apprehension
item.description:
It was raining in the Rohingya refugee camps in Bangladesh on Thursday, unusual for this time of year. One of my strongest memories of reporting on the 2017 exodus from Myanmar was the constant rain, turning jungle paths into muddy treachery.

But the drizzle didn’t stop hundreds of Rohingya men from gathering outdoors in front of a screen at 3 p.m. local time. In prayer caps and their finest clothes, they leaned in close to hear the International Court of Justice, which was issuing its ruling on whether Myanmar had committed genocide, define them as a distinct ethnic group that had suffered the gravest of atrocities: killing, sexual assault, the incineration of their villages.

Few of them spoke English, much less the legalese emanating from The Hague. Nonetheless, they watched.

Salauddin, 70, once a principal of a high school in Maungdaw Township, the site of some of the worst violence unleashed by Myanmar security forces, sat in the front row.

“I know it was genocide myself, and I hope that the court will say that,” he said.

As the legal proceeding dragged on, men left the viewing party at Jamtoli camp for the mosque. The call to prayer echoed. Such daily rites were banned by the Myanmar government in much of Rakhine State, the Rohingya homeland, one of many limits designed to erase the Rohingya identity.

The men wandered back. The judges were still talking. Nearby, vendors sold puffed rice and dried fish. Then the live broadcast cut off, and an announcement in the Rohingya language prematurely delivered the news: The court had recognized that Myanmar had committed a genocide against them. The explosion of cheers rivaled the biggest sporting match. Men wept. Everyone, it seemed, took selfies.

It took two and a half hours until the final verdict was read out.

The jubilation was electric. The announcer thanked everyone: the Bangladeshi government for hosting about 1.2 million Rohingya, 11 countries including the Maldives and Germany for adding their support to the case and, most of all, the African nation of Gambia that brought the genocide case against Myanmar on behalf of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation.

This was peak time to be Gambia. Rohingya boys and men gathered in a circle and jumped up and down, chanting in unison a single word: “Gambia.”

I asked one boy where Gambia was. Europe, he answered, though he said he wasn’t exactly sure. Regardless, it was a wonderful country, he said.

The crowds thinned. People walked through muddy alleys, night obscuring puddles, on their way back to their tarpaulin shelters in what is the world’s largest refugee settlement. Mohammed Yeasin Zuhar, 23, cradled his baby boy, only a month-and-a-half old, and said the ruling filled him with joy because his son might not have to grow up in these camps, these vast zones of insecurity.

Here, human traffickers kidnap children, and militants engage in running gun battles. An hour or so before the reading of the judgment began, I heard three gun shots pop nearby.

It was past curfew. I had to leave the camps. A group of Rohingya provided security, their arms spread to form a cordon around me, as a woman, their eyes searching for danger.

But refugees broke through anyway, with tales of woe — a family member killed, a sister raped, a child who didn’t survive the arduous escape from Myanmar. These tragedies continued after 2016 and 2017, the years ruled a genocide by the I.C.J.

I did not know what to say. I understood, like they did, that the court ruling might not change their lives anytime soon. Chances of the Rohingya returning home are slim. The court lacks enforcement powers.

The rain, though, had stopped.

item.title: Major Powers Vow to Increase Oil Supply Amid Global Energy Transition
item.description:
Among the four points the leaders of China, Russia and the United States agreed to on Thursday was a promise to work together to increase the production and supply of “refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.”

Their resolve is striking for a few reasons.

The wars led by two of them — Russia and the United States — have caused global oil prices to spike, creating a lot of economic pain for oil-importing nations. That has in turn accelerated their transition away from imported fossil fuel energy sources.

Electric vehicle sales have increased in many major markets, except the United States. And the International Energy Agency recently projected in an annual report that the world would add renewable energy capacity, led by solar, far faster over the next five years than it had in recent years because of what it called “unprecedented disruptions to global energy markets since the outbreak of the Iran war.”

“Renewables, already expanding at a record pace before the current energy crisis, are set to see strong growth across a wider range of countries around the world in the coming years as governments seek to strengthen energy security and reduce their exposure to imported fuels and volatile prices,” the agency said.

On Thursday, in its Energy Outlook Report, the agency went further, concluding that the war against Iran had permanently altered the appetite in many countries for imported oil, especially for oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy corridors.

How would the United States, Russia and China would increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products? That remains unclear. All three nations are refining powerhouses. But Russia’s refineries have been damaged in recent months by Ukrainian attacks. A significant amount of Russian crude oil is now being imported and refined in other countries, including China and India.

These three big countries have different agendas for how the world will be powered in the coming years. Russia and the United States are among the world’s biggest oil producers. They want fossil fuels to remain the main energy source of the global economy. China is leading the world to a very different energy future, one that relies on solar, wind, batteries and battery-powered vehicles for energy — all of which China dominates.

It is also striking that Thursday’s joint statement comes during global climate talks, where most countries (except the United States) have been discussing how to slow down global climate change, which is mainly driven by the burning of oil, gas and coal.

item.title: Trump Seeks to Project Power Abroad While Forced to Share It at Home
item.description:
This was the picture President Trump wanted for years: a trio of global titans sitting down together, just the three of them, a 21st-century conclave seemingly shaping the course of world events. At least in his eyes, it projected gravity, it projected grandeur, it projected power.

But the image of Mr. Trump flexing strength with his counterparts at a historic summit in China contrasted sharply with the drastically changing power dynamic for him back home. While he sought to use the meeting with the leaders of China and Russia to signal that he remains a giant on the international stage, Mr. Trump soon will have to share control with ascendant Democrats in Washington.

It says a lot about this president at this point in his rocky tenure that he would rather meet with President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia than with Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic congressional leaders who have yet to be invited to the White House since this month’s election. He offered hugs and arm pats and broad smiles to the autocrats, even as his administration has threatened criminal investigations of Democrats who pursue aggressive oversight of his administration next year.

“We are really making history,” Mr. Trump said with a note of pride at the beginning of the trilateral meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin here in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. As leaders of the big powers, he added, the three of them were addressing “issues impacting not just our people but the entire planet.”

He nodded to Mr. Xi. “It’s an honor for me to be with you,” he said. Then to Mr. Putin, he said, “It’s an honor for me to be with you.”

While a gripping photo op, the meeting produced no real breakthroughs, nor did it seem likely to lead to any. None of the traditional diplomatic spadework was done in advance to achieve concrete outcomes. And while the leaders issued a joint statement embracing goals like energy development and reduction of nuclear risks, it was not clear that sustained discussions would follow.

Instead, it was mainly an expression of power, which to Mr. Trump has always been the coin of the realm. Even after voters decisively repudiated him in the midterm elections, he has sought to reassert his authority by choosing a new might-makes-right White House chief of staff who has said that “the real world” is “governed by power.” In recent days, his secretaries of state and defense have questioned the extent that international laws apply to “men with swords,” which is, of course, how Mr. Trump and his testosterone-promoting team see themselves.

“The presidency, our presidency, is considered a strong presidency. You can do a lot,” Mr. Trump told CBS News on election night as voters were rejecting Republicans across the country, handing control of both houses of Congress to Democrats. Speaking with Fox News in Shenzhen on Thursday before his meetings, Mr. Trump emphasized that he will defy the new Congress. “They could do all the bills they want,” he said. “I just go veto, veto, veto.”

Unpopular presidents who lose control of Congress often turn to international affairs where they have more latitude to operate. Mr. Trump did not need congressional approval to meet with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. But with his Iran war stalled after nine months, Mr. Trump has less room to maneuver. And foreign leaders understand that he is now a lame duck who will be out of office in just over two years.

But the summit offered a welcome respite to Mr. Trump, who has long expressed admiration for authoritarian leaders like Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi, often applying the word “strong” to them, perhaps his favorite compliment. He has over the years talked enviously of their ability to get things done unburdened by the messy obstacles of legislatures and courts.

Indeed, Mr. Putin later suggested that he and Mr. Trump shared a common view of “civilizational values” and a “certain closeness” in perspectives. “For instance,” Mr. Putin told reporters after the meeting, “we were just discussing issues of democracy, right? But what is democracy, really?” He went on to suggest that “is, in fact, a liberal attempt to monopolize power — a liberal dictatorship, if you will.”

In his second term, Mr. Trump has endeavored to assert executive power to a far greater degree than in his first, asserting authority to sidestep Congress and the courts. He has taken an expansive view of his office, using the Justice Department to prosecute his personal enemies, gutting congressionally authorized agencies, firing theoretically independent officials and so on.

Asked in an interview with The New York Times in January whether he acknowledged any limits to his global power, he said: “Yeah, there is one thing. My own morality. My own mind. It’s the only thing that can stop me.”

Last month, he mused out loud to reporters in the Oval Office about how he could have used his power to go after Democrats like former Presidents Joseph R. Biden Jr. and Barack Obama and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, but chose not to. “I can do whatever I want, if I want,” he said.

Mr. Trump’s view of power goes back to his days in business. As a family-owned firm, the Trump Organization had no board of directors or shareholders to whom Mr. Trump had to answer. His decisions essentially were the final word. After he was inaugurated for his first term in 2017, he expressed shock that the government did not operate the same way.

He has surrounded himself with advisers who share his view of power, and his choice of chief of staff after his party’s disastrous midterm results made clear that he has no intention of backing down.

Stephen Miller, the new chief, has long voiced maximalist ideas about executive power. As a policy aide in the first Trump administration, Mr. Miller responded to a judge’s ruling striking down a ban on people from predominantly Muslim countries by saying that “the powers of the president to protect our country are very substantial and will not be questioned.”

In January, he dismissed talk of international law in discussing Mr. Trump’s desire to take control of Greenland. “We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else, but we live in a world, in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power,” Mr. Miller told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “These are the iron laws of the world that have existed since the beginning of time.”

Some other Trump advisers have worried Mr. Miller was going too far. As part of the president’s mass deportation blitz, Mr. Miller last year suggested suspending the constitutional right of habeas corpus and invoking the Insurrection Act to deploy the military to American streets in response to protests.

Will Scharf, then the staff secretary and now the White House counsel, wrote confidential memos objecting to both ideas, according to “Regime Change,” the recent book by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan of The Times. Both ideas were eventually put to the side, but never definitively ruled out.

But it is not as if Mr. Scharf is a dove when it comes to assertion of presidential power. Last week, he sent Democrats in Congress a letter warning that their efforts to investigate the Trump administration could be interpreted as intimidation and “may cross the line into blatant criminality” and “warrant further investigation.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio reflected the administration’s view about the reach of its authority during a recent speech to the Federalist Society denouncing the International Criminal Court, an institution that the United States has never joined but has become a particular target of Mr. Trump lately. Among other things, the court has issued an arrest warrant for Mr. Putin for alleged war crimes stemming from his invasion of Ukraine.

“If they’re foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans,” Mr. Rubio said of the international court, “our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general Pompey when he said to those who were trying to invoke their cities’ charters against his legions. He said, ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’”

“Not politically correct to say that,” he added, “but that’s what he said. That’s what he said.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth liked the idea so much that he posted a clip of Mr. Rubio online along with the line: “Stop quoting laws to MEN WITH SWORDS.”

If Mr. Rubio was making a somewhat nuanced argument that the international court’s jurisdiction — its “paper decrees” — did not apply to the United States, Mr. Hegseth seemed to take it one step further, disdaining the very idea of laws constraining military action.

Mr. Hegseth’s post generated criticism even from fellow conservatives who oppose American recognition of the International Criminal Court. Former Representative Justin Amash of Michigan, who left the Republican Party, called it an abandonment of the rule of law.

“Rejecting the ICC’s jurisdiction is one thing,” he wrote online. “Declaring that laws become irrelevant the moment swords appear is another. That’s just ‘might makes right,’ which is a fundamental rejection of both Christian ethics and America’s founding.”

In Shenzhen, Mr. Trump, Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin made clear where they stood on the idea of the reach of international law. In the joint statement they released afterward, they said that immunity of state officials is “of paramount importance.” On that, at least, the leaders of America, China and Russia were on the same page.

item.title: Trump Flaunts Camaraderie With Xi and Putin but Has Little to Show for It
item.description:
President Trump used his first-ever trilateral summit with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir V. Putin of Russia on Thursday to say that their respective nations were “uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on earth.”

But after an 80-minute conversation at a lakeside villa in the city of Shenzhen, a Chinese technology hub, it was unclear whether the three leaders had agreed to return to the kind of arms control talks that for decades were a centerpiece of diplomacy among superpowers during the Cold War. On new threats, including artificial intelligence, the three leaders were largely silent.

Mr. Trump, who also met with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin separately at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum this week, appeared delighted to convene the world’s largest nuclear powers for a discussion about disarmament. But he did not come with a detailed plan for how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons, or outline a path to one.

Instead, Mr. Trump relished what amounted to a high-profile photo opportunity of the three leaders seated around a circular wooden table. For Mr. Trump, the main achievement seemed to be a mutual commitment to keep talking about peace — without taking meaningful steps toward it.

“Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements, and we feel the opposite.” Mr. Trump told Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech.”

While China, which has the fastest-growing nuclear arsenal on earth, agreed to participate in the three-way discussion of nuclear weapons, the leaders announced little concrete beyond agreeing to continue a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. Mr. Xi has long been reluctant to agree to nuclear arms control because China’s arsenal remains a fraction the size of those belonging to Russia and the United States.

In the end, Mr. Trump’s whirlwind journey — two weeks after the Republican Party suffered a wipeout in the midterm elections and amid anxiety at home about widespread digital outages — amounted to a grand show of camaraderie.

As host of the tightly choreographed event, Mr. Xi flattered Mr. Trump and gave him an opportunity to ask for China’s assistance on matters ranging from ending global conflicts to spending more on U.S. agricultural goods. The summit also removed Mr. Putin from his status a global pariah over his invasion of Ukraine, elevating him to a leader deserving of equal diplomatic footing.

But for all of the talk of peace, there was no announcement of breakthroughs in the talks the Trump administration is engaged in to end that conflict. Nor did Mr. Trump appear to dwell on finding a way out of the its war with Iran.

“We don’t need any help,” Mr. Trump said, when asked by a Fox News reporter before the summit whether he would seek assistance from the other leaders in ending a conflict of his own making. In fact, the help Mr. Trump could ask for would involve demanding that China and Russia stop assisting Iran: U.S. intelligence has concluded that both countries provided either technology or targeting information that likely helped the Iranians strike American military bases in the Middle East.

On Fox News, Mr. Trump described the three-way conversation as a way to disrupt the growing “partnership without limits” that Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin say they have formed in recent years. Mr. Trump said that he hoped to break up that alignment and turn it into a three-way conversation, rather than a partnership focused on countering American influence.

China and Russia’s alignment, Mr. Trump said, “should have never been allowed to happen.”

Seeking his own path into Mr. Xi’s good graces, Mr. Trump has held three meetings with the Chinese leader this year, with the goal of cooling a tit-for-tat trade war and of building up a personal relationship through mutual flattery. Mr. Trump traveled to Joint Base Andrews to welcome Mr. Xi to Washington in May, and Mr. Xi responded in kind when Mr. Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday, treating the president to a military exercise and a fleet of U.S. and Chinese flag-waving dancers in a flurry of pink, blue and white outfits.

In Shenzhen, the heart of China’s robotics, telecommunications, semiconductor and software industries, Mr. Trump did not visit the chief technological competitors to the United States, or see coffee-serving robots near the city’s center.

Still, he marveled over the ceremonial welcome and held it up as evidence of a warming bond, telling an interviewer that “one of the great presidents of China” had greeted him. “He’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Mr. Trump said.

The president, who spends much of his time in the United States on bombastic appearances and incendiary social media posts, was on his best behavior alongside Mr. Xi. (He was his old self on Fox News before the summit, when he threatened to wipe out Iran should it attack the United States directly.)

Mr. Xi, for his part, said a much improved relationship between China and the United States in recent months was “the right way” for the two powers to “get along.” But he also warned that the key to keeping ties stable “lies in taking concrete actions to implement the consensus reached by the two heads of state.” The remarks came days after Washington moved to close a loophole on Chinese access to advanced A.I. chips.

As for Mr. Putin, the summit was his first encounter with Mr. Trump since the two men met in Alaska last year. That meeting was a diplomatic flop, and the war in Ukraine has intensified since then. The peace mechanism Mr. Trump advocated — a direct meeting between Mr. Putin and President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, moderated by Mr. Trump — has yet to materialize.

This time, White House officials were modest in their predictions. Expectations were set so low that White House officials who previewed the trip last week initially said that Mr. Trump would not bring up the war in Ukraine at all, although he ultimately did.

In Shenzhen, Mr. Trump continued welcoming Russia back into the fold of great superpowers. He called Mr. Putin “my friend,” and insisted that all three leaders would like to see the war end quickly. The Russian leader reiterated after the meeting, however, that he would not be negotiating with Ukraine.

During the trilateral meeting, Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin embraced the idea of peaceful leadership, without making commitments that would be much of a burden to either of their countries. In his own remarks, Mr. Putin said that their nations were “united not only by the status of being the victorious countries in World War II, but most importantly by the joint responsibility for maintaining international peace and security.”

And Mr. Xi mentioned a utopian goal that has pretty much fallen off the agenda of superpowers. He described nuclear weapons as a “sword of Damocles hanging over humanity” that should be eliminated. But Beijing has typically called on the United States to take the first steps in arms control, a demand that Mr. Trump seemed to acknowledge earlier in the day.

“For me, it’s a hard thing,” he told Fox News. “And it’s probably hard for them to do also.”

It has been done before, by Mr. Trump’s predecessors. Today, the United States and Russia each have slightly more than 5,000 nuclear warheads, and only 1,550 deployed under the New Start treaty that expired earlier this year — down from tens of thousands on both sides during the Cold War.

China, however, was never a party to past nuclear reduction treaties, and it is now intent on building up to at least current Russian and U.S. levels.

Mr. Trump also said in Shenzen that he wanted to crack down on nuclear proliferation by smaller powers — his justification for attacking Iran — and restrain what he said were the excesses of “rogue” organizations like the International Criminal Court.

Mr. Putin is subject to an I.C.C. arrest warrant over alleged war crimes in Ukraine. Nevertheless Mr. Trump welcomed the Russian leader in Alaska last year and extending an invitation to the Group of 20 summit next month in Florida. Mr. Putin told reporters after the meeting that he was unsure if he would attend.

One topic that went missing from each leader’s remarks was artificial intelligence, as China and the United States are locked in fierce competition over the new technology.

Mr. Trump did not answer a question, shouted by a Bloomberg News reporter at APEC earlier in the day, if the former chief executive of Nvidia — a company that has been central to the A.I. boom — had been disloyal to the United States. The executive, Jensen Huang, resigned after he was found to have two extramarital relationships, including one with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese asset.

The reporter who shouted the question was admonished by Chinese officials and barred from the trilateral meeting. Mr. Trump seemed blasé about the matter of espionage earlier in the day, telling Fox News that “we spy on them too.”

As the president basked in flattery from an authoritarian whose iron-fisted leadership he has openly admired, he gently suggested that he had not received as much media coverage as he would have liked.

“It’s too bad the media couldn’t see some of it,” Mr. Trump said of his trip.

David Pierson contributed reporting.

item.title: U.S. Auctions 31.5 Million Acres of Pacific Ocean to Deep Sea Mining Company
item.description:
In the first sale of its kind, the Trump administration on Thursday leased 31.5 million acres of the Pacific Ocean to a private deep sea mining company, despite a judge’s ruling this week that the auction would be illegal.

Only one firm bid to lease the seabed, which sits off American Samoa. The $6 million lease would allow the company to do mapping and other preliminary work but not actually mine the ocean floor for metals and minerals.

Administration officials would not disclose the identity of the successful bidder, saying it would be publicly released on Friday.

But Impossible Metals, a San Diego-based deep sea mining firm, had asked the government in April to hold the commercial auction. Company officials did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

The auction took place in Thousand Oaks, Calif., at a fire station near the regional office of the Marine Minerals Administration, a branch of the Interior Department that was created in July. Only two bidders showed up.

Outside the fire station, protesters marched and carried signs opposing the sale.

Deep-sea mining would involve scooping up nodules found on the seafloor that are rich in metals like cobalt, nickel, and manganese, which are important to manufacturing electric cars, batteries and other clean-energy technologies.

But mining the deep ocean has raised global opposition, and environmentalists argue that underwater plumes of sediment stirred up by mining machinery could devastate deep sea ecosystems.

More than 45 countries have called for a ban or pause on seabed mining, which currently does not exist in any commercial form.

But deep sea mining is a priority for President Trump, who last April signed an executive order that instructed the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to expedite approvals for mining companies.

Trump administration officials said the sale would benefit U.S. industries that rely on critical minerals.

“This sale is a critical first step in our offshore energy strategy,” said Michael Olsen, acting director of the Marine Minerals Administration. “It allows us to learn more about the resources in our offshore federal waters, and it enables us to assess whether those resources could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply.”

Whoever the winning bidder is might face an extended legal fight to start prospecting for those deep sea nodules.

On Monday, Judge Jill Otake of the U.S. District Court for the District of Hawaii ruled that the National Marine Fisheries Service “did not even attempt to consider” the potential harms to endangered marine species when it approved the planned sale, violating the Endangered Species Act. Mr. Trump nominated Judge Otake to the bench in 2017.

The proposed mining area is adjacent to the Rose Atoll National Marine Monument, a 13,500-square mile protected area known for its fragile pink-colored coral reefs, nesting areas for sea turtles, whales and other marine mammals, and more than 250 species of fish and seabirds.

Environmental groups said that the winner of the bid will face difficulty in pursuing a lease that has been ruled unlawful.

“There are a lot of problems with this sale,” said Erik Van de Stouwe, senior attorney for the Natural Resources Defense Council. “The investors of this bidder should ask a lot of hard questions given the court’s recent ruling.”

The N.R.D.C., Earthjustice and Finafinau, a youth-group based in American Samoa, sued the Marine Minerals Administration on Wednesday in federal court in Hawaii, asking the court to strike down any leases that the agency awards.

Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, said that although the mining lease is outside territorial waters of American Samoa, mining on the seafloor will stir up sediment and other pollution that spreads beyond the immediate area.

“We’re talking about sediment plumes, we’re talking about impacts on marine ecosystems that we completely don’t understand,” Ms. Suluai-Mahuka said in an interview. “How is that going to affect our corals. How is that going to affect other ecosystems that are already in place?”

Suluai-Mahuka said that many of the 49,000 island residents depend on the commercial tuna industry for their livelihood. They also depend on the ocean for their food. Both are at risk from commercial mining activity, she said.

“At a basic family level, we depend on whether or not we can feed ourselves from the ocean,” Ms. Suluai-Mahuka said. “You will see families fishing often, and eating the fish that they catch — it’s a daily way of people being able to feed their families. That hasn’t actually been factored in, either.”

American Samoa banned deep sea mining in 2024, citing “significant risks” to marine biodiversity, however its elected officials are split on the issue. On Monday, Gov. Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, a Republican, said he supported the sale.

“Today, we stand at the threshold of a new era of exploration, one that could unlock scientific knowledge, create economic opportunities, and strengthen American Samoa’s role in America’s strategic future in the Pacific,” the governor said in a statement.

Delegate Aumua Amata Coleman Radewagen, a Republican who represents the U.S. territory in the U.S. House, called the Monday ruling against the sale “significant” and said that she would reintroduce legislation to ban deep sea mining near American Samoa.

“We treasure our beautiful shores and waters, and we rely on a healthy ocean for fishing,” Ms. Radewagen said in an email to The Times.
