item.title: Love and Carjackings in a Video Game
item.description:
Full disclosure: I don’t play video games. I have never played video games. I did read a novel about video games once! (“Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow,” by Gabrielle Zevin. It’s good.)

But even I haven’t been able to avoid the cultural juggernaut that is Grand Theft Auto VI. This week, the legendary franchise released a new game after a 13-year hiatus, and it’s fair to characterize the response as rapturous. “The most extraordinary game I’ve ever reviewed,” one critic said. “The year’s signature cultural event,” one of our reporters wrote. Some are expecting the first week’s sales to approach $2 billion. “G.T.A. flu” — people planning to stay home from work or school to play — is a thing.

And so I called up my colleague Zachary Small, who reports on arts and culture (and also plays Grand Theft Auto). I wanted to ask him about the blockbuster cultural phenomenon known as G.T.A.

Zach, I am possibly the farthest thing from this game’s target audience. So explain to me: What’s the deal with Grand Theft Auto?

Today we think of Grand Theft Auto as very American, but it actually has roots in Scotland. It was this British take, in the form of a video game, on American crime movies — but the creators realized it’s a lot more fun to play as the bad guys than the good guys.

The Grand Theft Auto we know today unleashes players to wreak havoc across various fictional cities. You can steal cars. You can run over pedestrians. You can do a drug deal or get into a shootout with the police.

So what’s fun about it is that you can do crazy stuff that you can’t do in real life?

You’re thinking about it in the right way. But if you want a more philosophical spin on it, you could say that Grand Theft Auto is also commentary — that it offers this kind of satirical perspective on American culture, and what it means to try to achieve the American dream.

[Our colleague Joseph Bernstein has a great piece about how G.T.A. has always been a cartoonish parody of the United States — and how reality has now outrun the joke.]

Historically, there’s been a lot of pushback from educators and politicians against G.T.A. What were they worried about?

So a lot of the initial controversy around Grand Theft Auto was the developers’ own doing. It’s been reported that when the original came out in 1997, they paid P.R. companies to reach out to British tabloids and say, “Boy, this is a really controversial game; it’s super violent.” And, of course, that had the effect of making people want to play.

But later on, in the post-9/11 period, there were these fears about whether we’d become a violent society. And a lot of those fears became focused on video games and specifically Grand Theft Auto. And it became this sort of moral panic, based on research that today has been largely debunked.

You don’t really hear much of this in the response to G.T.A. VI.

Right, and I think that’s because this release comes at a moment when gaming as an industry is a lot more respected. The game is set in a fictional version of Miami called Vice City, and real elected officials in Miami are totally embracing it. The last time a G.T.A. was set in Vice City, there were protests and a lawsuit in Miami. So, there’s been this complete 180.

Why is that?

The series has been around for almost 30 years. A lot of people, including government officials, grew up playing these games, and feel nostalgia for them.

The game itself has also matured in this latest release. G.T.A. had been criticized for misogyny; one of the lead characters this time is a woman who is just as complex as her male counterpart. There’s romance. And, in addition to carjacking people, you can have your character engage in home repairs. So that’s one part of it.

The other part is the quality of these games, which is undeniable. The detail and the realism of G.T.A. VI is incredible.

Think about it this way. This game involves a lot of walking on the beach. Now think about how your foot hits the sand when you’re walking on the beach and how all the tiny pebbles move around as a result. For an animator, how many hours of work does that take? How much work just so a character can lean against a wall? Think about the physics of the clothes a character is wearing as he leans.

Now, think about the fact that in G.T.A. VI, you can go to the beach, and see different scenes unfolding everywhere you look. You can see a dog running into a wave. You can see people hitting a beach ball back and forth. And all of it looks incredibly realistic. The amount of work that takes cannot be overstated. All these thousands of tiny details have been taken into account by a team of almost 5,000 people, with a budget of more than $1 billion.

A huge amount of money and time went into G.T.A. VI. It’s also expected to generate huge sales. Where does the gaming industry go from here?

Yes, it’s going to make record amounts of money. But virtually no other studio in the video game industry could spend the money and time Rockstar Games took to make it. That was a huge risk. It’s going to be a hit, but that’s not a very sustainable approach. Imagine putting in that kind of investment and winding up with a flop. It’s hard to imagine we’re going to see many more of these sorts of prestige releases.

Are you going to play it?

I started this morning! So far I’ve gotten into a shootout, fenced some acid, and, of course, committed grand theft auto.

President Trump called Russia’s leader, Vladimir Putin, his “friend,” gushed about “making history,” and said the U.S., China and Russia should discuss reducing their nuclear weapons. But after the leaders of those countries held their first-ever trilateral summit, there were no breakthroughs on nuclear weapons, the war in Ukraine or confronting threats from A.I.

There is also little chance that the meeting will change the basic worldview of Putin and China’s leader, Xi Jinping. My colleague Edward Wong writes that Putin and Xi share a vision of transforming the world order by usurping the role of the United States as the sole superpower.

Anthropic had a roller-coaster first day on the stock market. Its shares surged more than 30 percent only to give up much of those gains, but it was still the biggest I.P.O. in history. The A.I. company is now worth about $2 trillion.

My tech reporter colleague Cory Weinberg explains in the video below how Anthropic’s stock market debut could affect its attempt to prioritize A.I. safety over profits.

The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims when, in a few weeks in 2017, it killed at least 10,000 people and forced three-quarters of a million people to flee.

An aerial attack by Yemen’s Houthi militia damaged the Riyadh skyscraper housing the offices of Saudi Arabia’s $900 billion sovereign wealth fund.

Iran has kept up its unrelenting attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz this week, including multiple strikes on the same tanker.

Around 92,000 people are attending the U.N. climate conference, which has ballooned into a trade show and networking opportunity, but the end result is expected to be modest.

A van Gogh sold for $190.4 million, setting an auction record for a work by the Dutch painter.

This question comes from a recent edition of the newsletter. Click an answer to see if you’re right.

Which actor was cast to play the next James Bond?

Tom Cruise

Robert Pattinson

Kit Harington

Idris Elba

Every mobile phone in South Korea buzzed loudly three times yesterday with an emergency alert — the kind typically used for a natural disaster or wartime catastrophe. But this alert was designed to expose would-be cheaters who brought their phones to the country’s notoriously grueling college entrance exam, known as the Suneung.

Fowl play: With cockfighting outlawed at home, American breeders are sending their roosters to the Philippines, which hosts international fights like the World Slasher Cup.

Who’s your daddy? A 300-kilo grizzly in the Canadian Rockies has become a celebrity. He is believed to have fathered many of the bears in Banff National Park.

Pika-ching! Pokémon cards are skyrocketing in value. Collecting them can turn into a lucrative career.

Also known as el pastel imposible (the impossible cake), chocoflan is a baking wonder from Mexico. Layers of chocolate cake batter and dulce de leche flan turn into a showstopper that is often served at parties.

Sitting on the Eurostar from London to Paris this week, the English Channel above me, I was hit by a wave of nostalgia.

After I moved from London to Paris in my early 20s, I took the Eurostar all the time. It all felt so familiar: the British and European sockets side by side, the Cheddar sandwiches and Perrier on the menu, the multilingual train personnel.

This was pre-Brexit, a time when Brits, like other Europeans, could just move to another European country and live and work there. Young Brits today can’t do what I did — or at least not as easily. (Young Europeans can’t easily move to Britain, either, but they still have the other E.U. countries to pick from.) Whatever you think about Brexit, one thing is worth noting: Young people voted overwhelmingly against it.

Young people frustrated at their lack of political power, especially in aging societies, have been a running theme in the news recently.

At the time of the Brexit referendum, a British friend told me that her dad, then in his 70s, had called her to ask how he should vote. He said he was in favor of Britain’s leaving, but realized this would affect her and her children more, and felt obliged to give her his vote.

I remembered that story when a French friend, whose teenage daughter is among the protesters at her Parisian high school, also said he would let her decide whom he should vote for in next year’s presidential election. “It’s about her future more than mine,” he said.

As it happens, my colleague Amelia Nierenberg is working on a story about Gen Z’s political hopes and dreams. If you’re 18 to 29, write to her here.

In the meantime, this week’s song is a bilingual collab between Zaho de Sagazan (French) and Tom Odell (British) called “Old Friend.” I love it.

Bon weekend! — Katrin

item.title: Unexpected Fallout From the Iran War
item.description:
Early this year, the start of the war in Iran caused what the International Energy Agency called “the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.”

Now, months later, the agency says some of the changes are permanent.

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” the I.E.A. executive director, Fatih Birol, said in a statement today alongside the organization’s annual World Energy Outlook.

My colleague Lisa Friedman wrote about the main takeaways for global energy markets. In short: Electrification is accelerating, drivers outside the United States are shifting rapidly to electric vehicles, and the extent to which the disruption reshapes energy policies will depend a lot on how long it lasts.

All of those changes have huge consequences for greenhouse gas emissions. So today, I’ll dive into the report’s climate implications.

The war in Iran has driven up gas and diesel prices around the world, making electric vehicles a more appealing and cost-competitive option. Globally, more than a quarter of the passenger cars sold this year will be full-electric or hybrid, the World Energy Outlook predicts. Electric vehicle sales have more than doubled in India, Australia and Brazil over the past year.

The United States has not kept up with the trend — E.V.s made up about 6 percent of domestic light-duty vehicle sales in the first eight months of the year, according to an analysis by the research group Ember. That adoption rate has been surpassed by 49 of the 56 countries where Ember tracks E.V. markets.

The report also finds that China is making real progress in electrifying heavy trucks. I wrote this year that electric big rigs have been slow to take off, largely because of high costs and charging obstacles.

In China, sales of electric trucks now make up about 35 percent of the new truck market, a rapid increase driven by government incentives and a business model that makes them more affordable.

Instead of buying trucks equipped with permanent batteries that need to be recharged periodically, operators in China are buying vehicles with batteries that can be swapped in a few minutes at roadside stations.

“You don’t have to pay for the expensive part of the truck, which is the battery,” said Dave Jones, chief analyst at Ember.

At the start of the war, a flurry of developments suggested that spiking prices for oil and gas imports could drive countries to embrace coal as a replacement.

Japan, Korea and Thailand delayed scheduled coal plant retirements and returned idle units to service. Italy postponed a planned phaseout. In September, my colleague Brad Plumer reported that the world was on track to burn record amounts of coal this year, largely because of fossil fuel shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

When burned, coal produces more planet-warming greenhouse gases than any other energy source.

The new I.E.A. analysis finds that the coal surge is temporary. It forecasts that coal use will be in decline globally by 2030 in all of the report’s projected scenarios.

The disruption of global oil and gas flows has caused countries that import energy to focus on producing more at home, the report found.

“The focus at the moment is just how expensive oil and gas is,” Mr. Jones said. “So everyone is trying to do whatever they can to replace oil and gas.”

In most places, that pivot is a boon for renewables and nuclear power.

“Encouragingly for the future, energy security and energy transitions have never been so closely aligned,” Mr. Birol said.

The I.E.A. modeled a range of scenarios for the future of oil and gas. Even in the one based on longer-term disruption of global oil and gas flows, the world is a long way from cutting emissions enough to keep average global temperatures below the threshold of 2 degrees Celsius that was established in the 2015 Paris Agreement, let alone the pact’s more ambitious 1.5-degree aspirational goal. The report also found that data centers could double global electricity use by 2030.

What does a video game need to accurately reflect America today? Sex. Violence. Phones. Drugs. Class struggle.

Grand Theft Auto VI, which came out this week, has all that. It also has finely realized depictions of every kind of extreme weather that is becoming more common because of climate change.

In Leonida, the game’s fictional world, which is modeled on Florida, there are tropical storms, torrential downpours, heavy winds and swampy afternoons. The game is also getting high marks for accurately representing biodiversity: There are manatees, alligators and 62 species of birds, including flamingos, gulls and pelicans.

While the weather doesn’t affect the plot of the game, it adds to the verisimilitude of G.T.A., and conjures a mood that, at times, is appropriately apocalyptic.

To better understand the environment in Leonida, I called my colleague Joseph Bernstein, who had early access to the game and spent the better part of the last month rampaging through Vice City.

Our conversation has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.

What’s the weather like in Leonida?

You can feel the humidity. It has that distinct quality to the air. You can smell the sea breeze, but it’s also like your shirt is sticking to your torso and you feel that.

How does the weather shape the atmosphere of the game?

One of the themes of the game is obviously excess. You are existing in this kind of heightened fun house, an over-the-top place. And the fact that Florida is beset by over-the-top weather that is obviously exacerbated by climate change is clearly part of the whole deal.

Previous installments of G.T.A. satirized America, and this one is much more realistic. How does the weather play into that?

It’s a part of the world that can’t be ignored. To not have it would be an oversight. You need it. It’s part of existence.

Interviewed by David Gelles

President Trump is asking the Supreme Court to let the E.P.A. cancel billions in Biden-era climate grants, The Associated Press reports.

item.title: Some Very Rare Cats Are Feeling the Heat in Turkey
item.description:
Outside, the sun beat down on the snow-capped mountains that ring the eastern Turkish city of Van. Inside the Van Cat Research Center on a November afternoon, the air-conditioning was on full blast — just to help a roomful of silky white felines keep their cool.

With their striking mismatched eyes of blue and amber, Turkish Van cats are the pampered royalty of the city that shares their name. They’re celebrated in local folklore, honored by a giant statue on the city’s main drag and protected by the Turkish government.

Yet, these iconic cats are feeling the heat. As climate change warms eastern Anatolia, the chief caretaker at the center said finding ways to beat the heat was now nearly a year-round concern.

“We never used to use air-conditioning here,” said Dr. Abdullah Kaya, a veterinarian and professor of biology who directs the research center, which is part of Van Yuzuncu Yil University. “But eventually, because of the rising temperatures, we had to install it,” he said.

Dr. Kaya called Van cats “cold climate animals,” and added, “In the past, the warm season was very short, but now it lasts much longer, and we’ve seen changes in both their skin and their fur.”

The center has successfully rescued the breed from the brink of extinction; fewer than 100 purebred Van cats could be identified in the 1990s. Today, more than 300 roam the facility.

Climate change is warming the eastern Anatolia region of Turkey faster than the global average, according to the United Nations climate science body. Van sits about 5,700 feet above sea level, a bit higher than Denver, and is seeing warmer winters, shrinking snowpack, irregular rainfall patterns and more frequent summer heat waves.

Lake Van, Turkey’s largest lake, also is experiencing an accelerating water crisis driven by shifting weather patterns combined with water mismanagement, said Caner Yerli, an associate professor of agricultural science at Yuzuncu Yil University. Climate modeling shows the Van basin is transitioning toward a hotter, drier Mediterranean-type climate, he noted.

The Van cats are built for harsh Anatolian winters, hence their longish, cashmere-like fur. Dr. Kaya said he has seen worrisome trends. The cats’ coats are thinning more severely in the summer. He’s also noticed significant appetite loss in the summer heat, causing the cats to lose weight.

But the Van breed has one climate adaptation option not available to other felines: their most un-catlike enthusiasm for swimming.

Over the years they have been observed paddling and even diving into Lake Van. Their fur has an unusual texture that repels moisture, like a natural parka that also helps keep them dry in damp or snowy conditions.

Now, when the weather is hot, they swim in specially designed pools at the research center.

“The pools can help reduce the effects of the heat, but of course, the real problem is that climate change is happening too quickly,” Dr. Kaya said. “We need to slow it down.”

The Van cat evolved over centuries in isolation in eastern Anatolia. They gained fame in the 1950s when two Britons writing about Turkey became enamored of them. In the late 1960s, the Van cat was officially recognized as a breed.

Around the same time, rapid urbanization in Turkey was replacing garden homes with multistory apartment buildings, eliminating much of their natural habitat. Some believed Van cats could not live in apartments and abandoned them. Purebred Van cats increasingly crossbred with domestic cats.

By 1992, a survey found only 92 pure Van cats remaining in the Lake Van region, prompting the state-backed university conservation program and government restrictions on taking them out of the country.

The push to save the Van cat is fueled by Turkey’s deep cultural affinity for felines. Here, street cats are neighborhood fixtures and treated like local V.I.P.s. They nap on shop counters, stroll through mosques, sun themselves on Byzantine walls and hop rides on ferries across the Bosporus. They’ve also made Turkey a font of viral online cat content.

There was Yesim, the tabby who became famous for waiting patiently in line at a butcher shop for his daily handout of offal, and Gli, the cross-eyed resident of Hagia Sophia in Istanbul who once charmed Barack Obama.

More recently, a stray ginger stole the show when it interrupted a performance of the “Romeo and Juliet” ballet by Prokofiev.

Yet while ordinary cats roam freely, purebred Van cats have become far too precious to leave to the elements. Today, they are rarely seen wandering the streets and instead almost all lounge indoors.

Dr. Kaya said his center has not been able to conduct a scientific study on how rising temperatures are affecting the breed, though he hopes to find a partner to pursue such research. Meanwhile, he said, the air-conditioned sanctuary offers a sobering warning for Turkey’s street cats.

“Even these cats, which live in a protected and controlled environment, are suffering from the heat,” he said, adding, “Imagine how much harder it must be for cats living outside without any protection.”

Ecehan Sirali translated interviews from the Turkish for this article.

item.title: The Rohingya Crisis Over the Years
item.description:
In 2017, Myanmar’s security forces started a swift, planned and brutal campaign of violence against Rohingya Muslims, an ethnic minority in the country that had already experienced decades of abuse.

Government troops and mobs rampaged through Rohingya communities, killing at least 10,000 people, destroying about 400 villages and carrying out systematized sexual violence, according to investigators with the United Nations.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya. It was the first time a state was held accountable for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The massacres catalyzed the rapid exodus of refugees as Rohingya people fled into neighboring Bangladesh. About 1.2 million of them still crowd precarious camps there.

Reporters and photographers for The New York Times covered that wave of attacks in 2017 as well as the systematic persecution of the Rohingya in the preceding years that had already forced many to flee.

item.title: Myanmar Genocide Ruling Sets Up Court Fight Over Israel and Gaza
item.description:
The landmark ruling on Thursday by the International Court of Justice that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims touched on some of the same issues as another case pending before the court: Israel’s war in Gaza.

It will likely be years before the court hands down a decision in the Gaza proceedings, which South Africa initiated in late 2023. But the judges who ruled on Thursday examined questions that are likely to arise in evaluating Israeli military conduct, including how to establish genocidal intent and how to assess mass killing that occurs while fighting militants.

While the 9-6 ruling by the United Nations’ top court in the Myanmar case largely tracked precedent in establishing genocide, the judges clarified “some of the questions that South Africa versus Israel could turn on” as that case is considered, said Janina Dill, an expert on international humanitarian law at Oxford University.

Whether Israel’s actions in Gaza amount to genocide is one of the most bitterly contested questions of the war that began when Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, killing up to 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and kidnapping roughly 250 hostages — the deadliest day in Israeli history.

The Israeli military response was devastating. More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed in airstrikes and a sweeping ground invasion in the three years since then, according to local health officials. Their tally does not say how many were combatants, but it includes thousands of children.

Israeli leaders fiercely dispute the charge of genocide, arguing that their war aimed to eliminate Hamas, not Palestinians as a whole. They say Hamas militants systematically operated from among Palestinian civilians, increasing the possibility that civilians would be harmed in attacks that targeted combatants.

Critics, including prominent rights groups like Amnesty International, argue that the killing of civilians and overwhelming destruction in Gaza crossed moral and legal red lines.

The cases brought against Myanmar and Israel both revolve around the question of whether they intended to exterminate a given group totally or partially. Leaders rarely announce explicit plans for mass murder, so international courts can reach that conclusion if, according to the law, it is the “only reasonable inference.”

The Myanmar genocide case was prompted by “clearance operations” in 2017, when the country’s security forces and ethnic Rakhine mobs rampaged through Rohingya communities, killing at least 10,000 people, according to U.N. estimates. The operation was collective punishment in response to attacks by Rohingya militants on police posts and a military base.

Similar to Israeli officials, Myanmar’s representatives argued in the court that their government had carried out a counterterrorism operation against Rohingya militants — the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, or ARSA — rather than genocide against civilians.

The International Court of Justice agreed that ARSA had likely carried out attacks on civilians. And the judges found that at least some of Myanmar’s so-called “clearance operations” were correlated with areas where ARSA was believed to have committed attacks.

But the court said Myanmar’s campaign went well beyond a counterinsurgency operation, including brutal attacks on fleeing civilians, widespread sexual violence, the methodical burning of villages, and the deliberate targeting of children, including babies.

The ruling emphasized that a response to an insurgency could still be “animated by genocidal intent,” Prof. Dill said.

The court split, however, over what evidence it should assess to determine whether Myanmar intended to commit genocide.

The majority of nine judges who ruled against Myanmar went beyond a 2015 I.C.J. ruling that focused on “the scale and allegedly systematic nature of the attacks,” among other factors. Relying on other international precedents, they also considered “the perpetration of acts that violate the foundations of the Rohingya group.”

The remaining six, who dissented, argued that the majority was using evidence — such as the history of discrimination against the Rohingya — which did not bear directly on the question of genocide.

“The Court’s new approach leads to a holistic assessment that is, in reality, so indeterminate that it borders on arbitrariness,” the dissenting judges wrote.

Yuval Shany, an international law expert at Hebrew University, argued that the Myanmar ruling could allow the judges weighing whether Israel intended to commit genocide to consider new kinds of contextual factors, creating more opportunities for South Africa to prevail.

“The standard has been very hard to meet until now, as Israel could point at alternative considerations explaining its conduct. But now there’s a whole other set of contextual factors which might need explanation, and it’s not clear exactly what the court will throw into the mix and how it will evaluate the totality of the evidence,” Prof. Shany said.

A cease-fire in Gaza last year reduced — but did not end — Israeli attacks in the enclave after two years of war.

A New York Times investigation in late 2024 found that the Israeli military had loosened guidelines instituted to limit harm to civilians to prosecute the campaign against Hamas.

That year, with the war at fever pitch, the court issued multiple orders instructing Israel to refrain from genocidal acts, to prevent and punish incitement and to take “all necessary and effective measures” to enable the provision of humanitarian assistance.

The orders did not establish whether Israel was committing genocide. The proceedings over that allegation are still ongoing. In March, Israel filed its “counter-memorial,” a formal, unpublished response to South Africa’s complaint.

Now, South Africa has until November 2027 to file its own rebuttal, after which Israel will have until 2029 to respond, according to a recent court decision.

item.title: After Bridge Attack, Putin Says He Will ‘Not Be Negotiating’ Ukraine Cease-Fire
item.description:
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia said on Thursday that “we will not be negotiating” any partial cease-fire with Ukraine after Kyiv’s attacks this week on the only bridge linking Russia to Crimea.

Mr. Putin publicly addressed the strikes, which destroyed a large part of the bridge that carried passenger vehicles, for the first time after a high-profile summit with President Trump and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen, China. He vowed painful Russian retaliation for the attacks.

The Russian leader built the bridge to connect Russia to Crimea in the years after Moscow illegally annexed the peninsula from Ukraine in 2014. It has served as a monument to Russian control over Crimea and to Mr. Putin’s larger imperial ambitions, as well as a crucial transport link for Crimeans.

Mr. Putin said that he had been discussing with his security council the possibility of a cease-fire on shipping in the Black Sea or a halt to strikes on energy infrastructure, but that any such possibility was now off the table.

“After these strikes on the Crimean Bridge, we will not be negotiating,” Mr. Putin said. He warned that Russia’s retaliation would “be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime has done to the bridge.”

Engineering specialists have said that work to restore the road part of the bridge could take years. Earlier this year, Ukraine tried to cut off Crimea to pressure Moscow to end the war.

Even before the bridge strikes, there was little sign that Mr. Putin was inclined to agree to any cease-fire in the coming weeks. Western intelligence assessments have found that the Russian leader plans to fight in Ukraine at least through the winter.

It was not immediately clear what the Russian leader’s statement meant for a large swap of prisoners of war and perhaps civilian prisoners that Mr. Trump’s special envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, helped negotiate at talks in Abu Dhabi last week.

But the announcement immediately dashed meager hopes that talks between Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen would lead to a breakthrough in the Trump administration’s on-again, off-again effort to end the war in Ukraine.

Russia has blamed various Ukrainian attacks for stalled progress on peace talks in the past, including a drone attack that Russia accused Ukraine of launching against Mr. Putin’s lakeside retreat but that Kyiv said never took place.

In his news conference in Shenzhen, Mr. Putin addressed the U.S. request to include European officials in the peace talks, which so far have been limited to Russians, Ukrainians and Americans.

He called insinuations by European officials that Russia was preparing to invade Europe “political diarrhea,” and reiterated his position that stationing Western troops in a postwar Ukraine was a red line that he could not tolerate.

But Mr. Putin also said that Moscow had invited European representatives to Moscow “through diplomatic channels” to clarify their position before determining any role for them in the talks. That statement suggested that the broader U.S.-led peace negotiations could continue, though it was unclear how serious the offer was.

Moscow has in the past rejected various European officials as unacceptable interlocutors, and Mr. Putin on Thursday said it would be impossible to normalize relations “without a change in the political elites in certain European countries.”

Mr. Putin raised doubts about whether he would accept Mr. Trump’s invitation to attend the Group of 20 summit in Miami next month. The Russian leader said Mr. Trump had brought up the question twice during their talks in Shenzhen.

No decision has been made yet, Mr. Putin said. But he added that he had to take into account what was happening in Russia, and that it was not always convenient for him to travel abroad. He said a high-level Russian delegation would attend if he did not go.

The Russian leader suggested that if Kyiv wanted to end the war, it should look at what Russia agreed to last year in Anchorage, Alaska, during a summit with Mr. Trump. At the time, Mr. Putin agreed to stop fighting if Ukraine handed over the rest of the eastern Donetsk region, a proposal that Kyiv rejected.

Oleg Matsnev contributed reporting from Munich.

item.title: 4 British Men Convicted of Sexually Assaulting Woman Drugged by Husband
item.description:
Four British men were found guilty on Thursday of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged her and secretly arranged for strangers to rape her while she was incapacitated.

It is the first time in England that a jury has convicted multiple defendants relating to drug-facilitated sexual assault.

The abuse of the woman, Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity under British law, spanned more than 13 years. Her husband, Philip Young, a former elected local official in the southwestern English borough of Swindon, pleaded guilty to 48 offenses, including 11 counts of rape, according to the Crown Prosecution Service.

Speaking after the jury’s verdict against the four men in the Winchester Crown Court on Thursday, Ms. Young said it sent a message to women and girls: that it is possible to “be believed and understood” in the British criminal justice system.

“It’s a relief not just for me and my family, but a relief for what this means for other women in the future,” she said. “It means that those who find themselves facing what I have are more likely to come forward.”

Two of the defendants were convicted of rape, and the other two of sexual assault. Sentencing was scheduled for December.

Mr. Young solicited the other men online, using platforms like Craigslist and Grindr, and arranged for them to visit the couple’s home in Swindon. In three of the four men’s cases, prosecutors had video evidence, filmed by Mr. Young, of Ms. Young drugged, blindfolded and restrained as the abuse took place.

The four men argued in court that they had believed that Ms. Young had consented to the encounters based on assurances from her husband. The jury found that was not enough, and that the defendants — Connor Sanderson-Doyle, Richard Wilkins, Norman Macksoni, and Mohammed Hassan — had failed to establish legal consent.

Ms. Young’s case echoed that of Gisèle Pelicot, the Frenchwoman whose husband also drugged and raped her repeatedly and invited dozens of men into their bedroom to do the same. That abuse began in 2010, but Ms. Pelicot did not learn of it until 2020.

She decided to come forward, prompting a national reckoning in France, and inspiring women across the country to rally around her and demand a change to the country’s consent laws. In 2024, 51 defendants were found guilty of assaulting her.

item.title: Myanmar Committed Genocide Against the Rohingya, Top Global Court Finds
item.description:
The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, a landmark decision years in the making that makes the Southeast Asian nation the first state to be held to account for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The ruling covers Myanmar’s deadly military campaign against the Rohingya minority, which killed at least 10,000 people in a few weeks in 2017 and forced three quarters of a million people to flee during that same period. More deaths and expulsions followed.

“The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine state,” Judge Yuji Iwasawa, the president of the I.C.J., said while reading the court’s decision on Thursday. The decision was made by 9 votes to 6.

The decision could have sweeping implications, including for another genocide case before the I.C.J., the United Nations’ highest judicial body: the accusation of genocide by Israel against the people of the Gaza Strip.

A spokeswoman for the government of Myanmar, in the capital Naypyidaw, did not answer a phone call seeking comment after the verdict was handed down. Myanmar authorities have previously disputed the charge.

Among other findings, the court determined that Myanmar had failed to prevent genocide. While it was not found to have incited private people to commit genocide, the court found that it also failed to punish genocide.

“This is a case a decade in the making,” said Juliette McIntyre, a Senior Lecturer in Law at Adelaide University in Australia. “From the point of view of the Rohingya people, who have been waiting, and waiting, and waiting for justice, this is very important.”

Gambia filed suit against Myanmar in 2019 in the court, which is based in The Hague. While the West African country is thousands of miles from Myanmar, international law gives countries the ability to act against genocide anywhere in the world — even if they are not affected.

In the Jamtoli camp of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, people thronged to a public viewing party to watch the hourslong decision, cheering and weeping as the decision was read. Some held signs that said “thank you, Gambia.”

In The Hague, Dawda Jallow, the attorney general for Gambia, welcomed the decision to find Myanmar culpable of the “crime of crimes.” Speaking to journalists on the main staircase of the I.C.J.’s Peace Palace shortly after the ruling was read, he said, “we will stand with the Rohingya until justice is served.”

The violence at the core of the case took place in Myanmar’s far western Rakhine state, starting in 2016 and worsening in 2017. U.N. officials and human rights groups have called it a coordinated, scorched-earth campaign to remove the Rohingya — one that involved killing, wounding and raping, razing villages, and eventually forcing the expulsion of more than a million people to neighboring Bangladesh.

The Rohingya Muslims have a long history of repression in Myanmar. After the nation’s independence from Britain in 1948, they were one of many ethnic groups in the country, which was then known as Burma. But over time, they faced increasing attacks from members of the nation’s Buddhist majority.

A restrictive citizenship law in 1982 effectively rendered most Rohingya stateless. Various Myanmar governments, including a civilian authority led by the Nobel peace laureate Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, have refused to even acknowledge the Rohingya as a legitimate ethnic group, falsely referring to them instead as interlopers from neighboring Bangladesh.

Myanmar’s military called its campaign against the Rohingya “clearance operations.” Ms. Aung San Suu Kyi defended the military at the I.C.J., denying it committed genocide, before her government was deposed by the military and she was imprisoned in 2021. (After the coup, Myanmar descended into a civil war that is still raging.) About 1.2 million Rohingya now live in dire conditions in overcrowded camps in Bangladesh. Following the eruption of Myanmar’s civil war in 2021, much of the Rohingya homeland is now controlled by a milita from the Rakhine ethnic minority, which has also been accused of persecuting Rohingya.

Thursday’s decision hinged on whether Myanmar acted with the specific intent to physically destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part, as an ethnic or religious group.

The court found that Myanmar took measures to wipe out the Rohingya people, who did constitute a protected ethnic group by the court’s judgment.

The case summary states that, among other atrocities, the court found that “widespread acts of extreme violence were perpetrated by the Myanmar security forces against children in northern Rakhine State,” that “in addition to the extreme hardship of the journey, the Myanmar security forces systematically shot at Rohingya as they were fleeing,” and that “the evidence demonstrates a deliberate, organized process” of destroying Rohingya villages.

“The only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the group,” Judge Iwasawa read from the ruling.

The court said that Myanmar must provide restitution — trying to put things back as they were, including through allowing return and reunification — and, where that fails, compensation. But the amount of compensation needed is not yet set, and will be determined in further proceedings.

The court does not have the power to enforce its own rulings, and the U.N. Security Council would need to uphold the decision. Two members of the Security Council, China and Russia, may opt to protect Myanmar. Each provides Myanmar with weapons it now uses to kill civilians in the civil war.

“Concerned governments” should “press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch, said in a written statement following the announcement.

Notably, the United States has previously said that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, though that happened during the Biden administration.

“I think that you’re going to see relatively powerful states putting pressure on Myanmar,” said Ms. McIntyre, of Adelaide University. “How much they pay heed to that pressure is a question.”

Thursday’s decision was greeted by some in the international legal community as a sign that justice can still be served on a global stage, even as the Trump administration attacks international bodies. The administration plans to impose sweeping sanctions against another tribunal, the International Criminal Court, which could severely impair the court’s ability to function on a day-to-day basis.

“At a moment when international law and the institutions that uphold it face growing pressure, the Court’s decision reaffirms the vital role they play in establishing truth,” James Goldston, the executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, said in a statement.

For the Rohingya now in Bangladesh, the news was welcome. Yet tragedies continued after 2016 and 2017, the years ruled a genocide by the I.C.J.

Mohammed Yeasin said his wife and sister were killed in a drone attack in August 2024. The perpetrators were not the Myanmar military but the armed group from the Rakhine ethnic minority that shares its homeland with the Rohingya.

“I am happy about the I.C.J.,” he said. “But I don’t know when my sorrows will end.”

Jonathan Wolfe, Marlise Simons and Saikou Jammeh contributed reporting.

item.title: Wreck of First Australian-Built Warship Is Revealed 128 Years After It Sank
item.description:
Maritime archaeologists and navy divers have located the wreck of the first Australian warship 128 years after it sank, Australia’s Defense Department announced this week.

The authorities and scholars said the discovery of the wooden gunboat, Spitfire, was particularly significant because it was the first warship to be built in Australia in the 1800s under the British colonial government. The ship was constructed in Sydney and launched in 1855. It sank during a cyclone more than 40 years later near the Piper Islands in the Great Barrier Reef.

The wreck site of the 52-foot vessel, made of ironbark and blackwood with copper fastenings, was located in August off the northern state of Queensland after a monthlong expedition that involved a minehunter vessel, remotely operated vehicles and a navy dive team.

An “acoustic anomaly” caused by the wreck was detected by a sonar team, leading to the discovery, the announcement said. Clearance divers with the Australian Navy, specialists who typically deal with underwater demolitions and explosive ordinance removal, then documented the parts of the wreck that were exposed above the seabed, according to maritime archaeologists involved in the search.

Spitfire was commissioned by the state government of New South Wales, where Sydney is located, to protect the city against Russian warships based in Vladivostok, according to the Australian navy. After serving as a patrol boat and pilot vessel, the ship was sold off into private ownership and was used in commercial fishing in the trade for bêche-de-mer, or sea cucumbers.

The site of the wreck is protected as underwater cultural heritage under Australian law.

item.title: After Brexit, Baby Steps to Bre-entry? What to Expect at U.K.-E.U. Summit
item.description:
British and European leaders are set to meet in Brussels on Friday to remove some barriers introduced by Brexit, a decade after U.K. voters decided to leave the now 27-nation bloc.

The reset has been reinvigorated by Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, who declared this week that Brexit “has not worked.” “It’s like the Emperor’s new clothes, where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth,” Mr. Burnham said in a speech Monday, adding: “To be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years.”

Many hurdles stand between Britain and a dramatically closer relationship with Brussels, but officials are slowly chipping away at their differences. This is the second summit focused on closer collaboration.

Here’s what to watch for.

The goals of the one-day summit are specific, and fairly modest. They are the result of months of diplomatic work that began when the previous Labour prime minister, Keir Starmer, entered office and began pursuing closer ties with Europe. They include:

An agreement to relax restrictions on agricultural trade. This would help British farmers, who have complained since Brexit about the paperwork required to sell goods to the E.U.

A “youth experience” program. This would allow tens of thousands of young people in Europe to temporarily work and study in Britain — and vice versa — without the restrictions put in place after Brexit.

A deal to realign their carbon emissions trading systems, with a goal of making it easier and cheaper for businesses to deal with environmental regulations.

Some changes introduced after Brexit are not being discussed:

Freedom of movement is still off the table. Britons and Europeans used to have quicker and easier checks at one another’s borders. And European and British workers cannot move between jobs in Britain and on the continent as easily as they could before Brexit.

Trade talks remain different. Britain negotiates and strikes its own trade deals post-Brexit, whereas in the European Union, trade policy is made by the bloc.

In Britain, the shift in tone is coming from the top.

“After 10 years,” said Nathalie Tocci, an Italian political scientist at Johns Hopkins, “there is a prime minister who is prepared to recognize openly what everyone has known for 10 years: that Brexit was a huge, excuse my Oxford English” — finishing the thought with an expletive.

That opens the door to a serious conversation about the future of Britain’s relationship with the European Union, she said.

The reset is also heavily informed by three countries not in the room.

President Trump has spent two years upending global trade with tariffs, prodding Europe to take more responsibility for its own defense, cozying up to Russia and surprising allies. That has pushed America’s closest partners to look for friends elsewhere.

Europe and Britain both face economic risks from China’s exports and the race between the Chinese and the United States for artificial intelligence dominance. And Russia’s continued aggression against Ukraine has underscored the need for defense preparedness.

Britain’s E.U. reset is “a reaction to Donald Trump, but not only: It’s also about a recognition that in a less rules-based world, you need to have a critical mass,” said Fabian Zuleeg, chief executive of the European Policy Center, a think tank.

Polling suggests that a clear majority of Britons now think Brexit was a mistake. But even some Labour officials admit they are wary of another acrimonious debate.

They also fear that moving closer to Europe could benefit Nigel Farage, the pro-Brexit leader of Reform U.K., and Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the Conservative Party. Both politicians are eager to revive the fights over immigration and British sovereignty that powered the Leave campaign.

Even those who support closer ties between the bloc and the U.K. suggest that nothing about a second political marriage will be easy.

“When Brexit was decided on by a referendum, there was a lack of clarity as to what exactly that meant,” Sonja Hyland, Ireland’s ambassador to Britain, said at an event at Chatham House in London this week. That makes it hard to negotiate.

While Mr. Burnham has cracked the door open to Britain possibly rejoining the bloc one day, he insists that he will only present options to the public, and that any decision would take place after the next general election. “At every stage, the British people will be the boss,” he said.

Any move to rejoin the European Union — or even just the customs union, or a bespoke and close relationship that looks more like the one the bloc has with Switzerland — could take years. It took more than five for Britain to leave.

It is also unclear how the bloc would approach a bid to rejoin, especially following a series of elections next year.

“As much as people might miss the U.K., there is also very much a sense of: Well, you’ve left, and we’ve had to get on with it,” said Rebecca Christie, a senior fellow at Bruegel, a research institute.

Megan Specia contributed reporting.

item.title: A Summit Gives Putin the Win He Craves: Equal Stature With Superpowers
item.description:
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia stood shoulder to shoulder for the cameras with the leaders of the two global superpowers. He was publicly praised by one of them, President Trump, as “my friend.” And he proclaimed, in between meetings with at least seven world leaders over two days, that efforts to isolate his nation had failed.

Mr. Putin emerged as the big winner after a meeting on Thursday with Mr. Trump and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, during a summit in Shenzhen, China. The Russian leader walked away with a symbolic triumph in his quarter-century battle to restore Russia’s place as a great power at the fulcrum of world affairs.

Appearing alongside Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi, the two leaders most responsible for helping him escape isolation since his invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Mr. Putin showed that he could be embraced by the powers that matter most without making any compromises on the war.

“It ends the isolation that at least the West tried to impose on him after the full-scale invasion,” said Angela Stent, a Russia expert and senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. “There he is. He is meeting with Xi and Trump, and so much for isolation and sanctions.”

The trilateral meeting — the first of its kind between the three countries — amounted largely to diplomatic theater that elevated Russia beyond its status. Russia lags both the United States and China in economic clout, population size and most other major metrics of influence.

The big exception, apart from landmass and certain natural resources, is nuclear weapons. Russia retains the world’s largest arsenal, an inheritance from the Soviet Union, and Mr. Putin ensured that was not lost on any of the attendees.

Hours before Mr. Putin arrived at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Russian strategic nuclear bombers landed in Vietnam for the first time since the Soviet era. In Shenzhen, a prominent pro-Putin commentator was filmed incredulously approaching the Russian officer carrying the “cheget,” the nuclear command-and-control device that travels everywhere with the Russian leader, and asking: “Is that the nuclear briefcase, the very one?”

Mr. Putin had not shown up in person for the annual APEC summit in nine years. The in-person event was canceled from 2019 to 2021. The United States, which played host in 2023, did not invite him because of the war in Ukraine, and an international warrant for his arrest over the transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia complicated visits to Peru and South Korea in 2024 and 2025.

But on Thursday, the Russian leader was granted a place on a red-carpeted stage with his American and Chinese counterparts, even as he has escalated his war against Ukraine, killing record numbers of Ukrainian civilians and playing hardball during the Trump administration’s renewed efforts to end the conflict.

During the meeting and afterward, the Russian leader and Mr. Trump railed against the International Criminal Court, which issued the arrest warrant for Mr. Putin. Mr. Trump called the institution, which his administration has punished with sanctions, an out-of-control “rogue globalist organization.”

While Russia basked in the diplomatic pomp and pageantry, Ukraine brought a reality check. Just hours before the trilateral meeting, Ukrainian forces for the third time in a week struck the bridge connecting Russia with Crimea, the peninsula that Mr. Putin illegally annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

Past American presidents have been wary of conferring legitimacy on autocrats actively opposing U.S. interests, but Mr. Trump agreed to the summit with Mr. Putin without forcing any prior commitments regarding Ukraine.

In a news conference afterward, Mr. Putin said he and Mr. Trump shared a common approach to “civilization values” and had a “similarity of views,” citing a recent discussion about democracy.

“What exactly is democracy? What is it?” Mr. Putin asked. “Is it the liberal order that certain circles have sought and are still attempting to impose on the entire world, fashioned according to their own blueprint? Is that democracy or is that a liberal attempt to monopolize power — in fact, liberal dictatorship?”

The formal statement that the three world leaders issued after their meeting made no mention of the conflict in Ukraine, though Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump discussed the topic in talks before the trilateral summit.

During his news conference, Mr. Putin said that, in response to Ukraine’s attacks on the Crimea bridge, he was ruling out any maritime or energy infrastructure truce with Kyiv, and would mete out a painful retaliation.

There had been few signs that such limited cease-fires were in the offing, anyway. At peace talks last week in Abu Dhabi, led by Mr. Trump’s special envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Russian negotiating team reissued hard-line demands from five years before.

Mr. Putin said that, at the insistence of the United States, he had invited European officials to Moscow “through diplomatic channels” to ascertain their position and decide if they should be included in talks. The negotiations up until now have included only the United States, Russia and Ukraine.

Ukraine and European nations have said repeatedly that they must be involved in any discussions about their security. In an interview with NBC News ahead of the summit, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said that “big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world, but it’s a huge mistake, absolutely.”

Mr. Trump and Mr. Putin, however, appear to share the opinion that “there are only a few really serious players” in world affairs that matter, said Ms. Stent, the American Enterprise Institute fellow.

“Trump is obviously a completely different president,” she said. “He is happy to be seen with these authoritarian leaders. He really is not interested in being seen with American allies, either European or Asian.”

Asked whether Thursday’s summit amounted to a new Yalta — the World War II conference where Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin brokered the fate of postwar Europe — Mr. Putin replied: “What was so wrong with Yalta?”

He said Yalta finalized the victory over Nazism and paved the way for the United Nations, skipping over how the negotiation set the stage for millions of Europeans to be swept behind the Iron Curtain.

For years, a leading raison d’être of Mr. Putin’s rule has been to reverse the decline of Russian power that came in the aftermath of the Soviet Union’s collapse, which he famously called “the greatest political catastrophe of the century.”

“We showed ourselves to be weak, and the weak get beaten,” Mr. Putin remarked in a 2004 speech after a terrorist attack at a school in Beslan. He seethed with disgust at how vulnerable Russia had become and set the wheels in motion to consolidate domestic political control.

Mr. Putin viewed Moscow’s loss of power as demeaning and humiliating, chafing at the way he was treated as a second-tier leader by American officials. For much of the 1990s and 2000s, U.S. leaders did not regard Moscow as a force to be reckoned with or feared in global affairs.

Over the years, the Russian leader tabulated the slights, growing more intent on ending what he has long called the “unipolar world,” his chosen term for a world he said was unfairly dominated by the United States. Those politics of grievance fueled his increasingly bold and deadly drive to restore Russian might.

Even after Thursday’s summit accorded him the trappings of a superpower leader, Mr. Putin spent part of his news conference saying he was not responsible for invading Ukraine, instead blaming prior Western elites.

“They didn’t give a damn about our opinion, because they believed that there was nothing left to negotiate with Russia. You just have to push,” Mr. Putin said during his news conference on Thursday. “Well, they brought this pressure to the point of hostilities and war.”

item.title: Gen Z Is Driving Global Political Change, Aiding Far Left and Far Right
item.description:
Thousands of students are poised to hold simultaneous and coordinated protests in several European countries on Friday, demanding an end to war, to social-welfare spending cuts and, in some cases, to capitalism itself.

It is the latest iteration of the global youth uprisings that have spilled through streets from France to India this year, and helped to power recent election upsets across Europe and the Americas.

Polling shows that frustrated young people played a disproportionately large role in voting out nationalist leaders in Hungary and Serbia, in electing the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction, and in putting a German far-right party on track to govern a German state for the first time since World War II. They could prove crucial in upcoming elections in France and Spain.

“It’s becoming harder and harder to not connect all of the different issues facing our generation,” said Adam Powell-Davies, 27, the national chair in Britain of the Socialist Students, one of the groups organizing Friday’s protests. “Not just in specific countries, but globally.”

The beneficiaries of this youth anger are ideologically diffuse. They include centrists — as well as insurgent politicians on the far left and on the far right who offer stark and social-media-friendly solutions to the ailments of an unsettled global order.

Organizers and experts say the connective tissue between these spasms of youth anger is a frustration with established political power structures, whatever their ideological bent — and a perception that economic opportunity is slipping away from young people.

A decade of pandemic, war, warming temperatures and a generation-defining fiscal reckoning in wealthy economies have combined to fuel fears that young people may never enjoy the peace, prosperity and freedoms of their parents and grandparents. Countries like France are struggling with high government debt and face difficult choices for how to maintain the promises of generous social welfare systems.

“There’s no future for us,” Laura Spearey, a 27-year-old information technology student from Bilbao, Spain, who traveled to Britain to join the Friday protests, said in an interview.

She cited difficulties in securing housing, health care and other necessities of adulthood: “You have no chance whatsoever to have your own life, to build your life project.”

Those anxieties have persisted for years: They also drove the “Occupy” protests that followed the 2008 financial crisis. But survey data suggests they are growing more urgent, even in countries, like Germany, where youth unemployment rates are still lower — and there is less government debt — than in Britain and France.

In Germany, young people’s economic concerns have grown in the past decade, according to “Youth in Germany,” an academic study that has surveyed more than 2,000 young people per year over nine years.

“The crucial question is not simply whether today’s young people are objectively worse off than previous generations,” said Klaus Hurrelmann, a professor of public health and education at Berlin’s Hertie School and a co-author of the “Youth in Germany” study. “What matters is that many of them are beginning to believe that the traditional promises of our society no longer apply to them.”

Across much of Europe, that belief has been further fueled by governments’ promises to spend more and more on national defense in the years to come, both to compensate for declining American military support for the continent and to counter threats from Russia. Younger protesters have called for a reversal of that buildup, saying it drains needed money for education, health care and other social services.

In Germany, many protests groups say they have been galvanized by government efforts to encourage young people to sign up for military service in an effort to bolster fighting forces, a move that many young people worry will lead to a military draft.

In a list of demands published ahead of Friday’s protests, one of the German groups organizing the events, “Gen Z Regelt” — roughly translated, “Gen Z Gets Things Done” — called for the resignation of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has taken the lead in ramping up German military spending. It also says “not one person, not one cent, for the German armed forces.”

The group’s demands, like the others behind Friday’s events, skew sharply to the left. They critique the capitalist system. They notably refrain from taking aim at older generations that have benefited from opportunities that they fear they are missing out on, like buying homes and securing generous pensions. Instead, they frame the conflict as workers versus the rich and powerful.

“It’s not a battle of the young versus the old,” said Hannah Ponting, 20, a member of the Socialist Students at Liverpool University, who is helping to coordinate protests there. “Neither of those groups are controlling where this money’s going.”

In Berlin in September, similar sentiments — and a surge of voting from people as young as 16 — helped the far-left party Die Linke score an upset victory in the city election.

In other parts of Europe and the world, though, the anxiety has driven young voters to the far right as well as the left.

According to recent polling in France, roughly one in five of voters aged under 25 says they will vote for the main far-right party in next year’s election, and an even higher proportion voted far-right in French legislative elections in 2024.

In the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, exit polls showed the far-right Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, won more than 40 percent of the youngest voters in a state election in September — more than double the share for any other party. The AfD’s main candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is a telegenic TikTok star who promised to restore opportunity for the state, by deporting some immigrants, providing new benefits to young parents and ending German support for Ukraine.

The success of the AfD and Die Linke in Germany illustrates how quickly young voters are willing to turn on political parties that promised rapid change but failed to deliver, said Mr. Hurrelmann of the Hertie School. Just five years ago, young Germans flocked to centrist parties in a national election.

The centrists have now lost out to the AfD and Die Linke, which have promised radical change by shunning the compromise-driven model of governance that has long dominated German life.

“They are completely free to promise everything,” Mr. Hurrelmann said, “because they are not now in a position to deliver.”

Mainstream parties have few incentives to meet young people’s demands, because doing so risks alienating the older voters who make up the majority of their coalitions, said Tim Vlandas, a professor at Oxford University who studies the political consequences of aging populations.

If the far left or far right were to take power, he added, they would likely face similar pressures — because they would also have to appeal to older generations to stay in government.

Such a cycle, he said, would just increase pressure on young people to take to the streets. “When you don’t influence politics, you can protest. You can become alienated and stop voting,” he said. Or, he added, “you can radicalize.”

item.title: Victims of Clerical Sexual Abuse Want More From Pope Leo
item.description:
Among the millions of people who looked forward to Pope Leo XIV’s visit to South America were survivors of clerical sexual abuse who hoped his presence might spur greater accountability for the abusers.

Instead, the trip, which concluded this week, has left them disappointed. They say the pope has not done enough to change the Roman Catholic Church’s approach to sexual abuse and lament how Leo met with only a relatively small number of victims, who were selected through a secretive process.

The frustration in South America reflected broader accusations throughout parts of the Catholic world that Leo, who was elected pope in May 2025, has not acted fast enough to ensure justice for victims or implement more safeguards to prevent future sexual abuse by priests. A papal commission that Pope Francis established in 2014 to develop protocols for protecting minors from clerical abuse presented its interim proposals to Leo this year, but the pontiff says that they need to be reviewed and finalized before being published.

“We haven’t seen him lift a single finger with the intention of changing anything within the Catholic Church’s system,” said José Enrique Escardó, the founder of a victims’ support group who said he was abused by members of an ultraconservative Catholic group disbanded by Pope Francis.

Leo, as a bishop in northern Peru, helped the group’s victims obtain mental health counseling and financial payments but, Mr. Escardó said, has not adequately built on that work as pontiff.

Leo has made “only pastoral statements, responses to journalists’ questions and staged meetings with victims,” Mr. Escardó said, adding that he wanted the pope to ensure that all abusers were prevented from serving in the church.

The Vatican declined to comment on the accounts and accusations in this article. Speaking publicly during the trip, Leo addressed the matter in general terms without outlining specific plans. He told bishops in Lima, Peru, that the Church must respond to clerical sexual abuse “with truth, justice, forgiveness, making amends and an evermore resolute commitment to fostering a culture of prevention and protection for the weakest in light of such crimes.”

He also spoke individually in Buenos Aires and Lima with 11 abuse survivors after meetings with other victims in France and Spain this year. According to Vatican statements, the pope heard testimonies of all 11 and was committed to the “creation of safe environments.”

A much larger number of victims had requested to meet with him, but Catholic officials said he could only meet with some because of the hectic schedule during his 12-day visit to the continent. “Naturally, he has to manage this himself, which means making selections, because he doesn’t have much time,” Cardinal Carlos Castillo, the archbishop of Lima, told a local journalist in Peru.

The Vatican’s refusal to explain how it selected the victims who met with the pope has created unease among abuse victims and campaigners. “We don’t know who they met with, who the abusers were or if they were brought to justice,” said Sergio Salinas Giordano, the global director of Ending Clergy Abuse, an international survivors’ group.

Ana María Quispe, 30, was among the abuse survivors who was not invited to meet the pope on this visit.

She has previously accused Leo, when he was a bishop in Chiclayo, Peru, of allowing a priest who she said abused her as a child to continue in his role amid an official inquiry. A New York Times investigation in 2025 uncovered images that showed the priest participating publicly in Mass during the inquiry, contradicting the Church’s announcement that he had been suspended.

Ms. Quispe said she rejected the presentation of the pope as an advocate for abuse victims. “It outrages me; it even disgusts me,” she said in an interview.

The Vatican previously said Leo’s investigation into the priest went “beyond the prerequisites” and closed it because of a lack of evidence, citing the civil authorities’ decision to drop the case.

During an interview, Ms. Quispe was teary, her voice breaking frequently. She said the feeling of not being heard by the Church was more painful than the abuse she experienced as a child. “That’s what destroyed me,” she said. She has been seeking a public apology for her case, Ms. Quispe said, as well as reparation payments for all victims and outside oversight of the Church.

Reinaldo Nann, who was the bishop of Caravelí, Peru, from 2017 until 2024 before resigning to marry a woman, said bishops sometimes did not want to punish the priests they oversee.

“Bishops are given an amount of power that can only be equated with feudalism,” Mr. Nann said. Since the Vatican relies on bishops for information about abuse cases, he said, a bishop can stymie an investigation by withholding evidence. “That is a systemic problem,” Mr. Nann said. “I do not expect changes from Pope Leo on that issue.”

The Church under Leo’s predecessors, Pope Benedict XVI and Pope Francis, was notoriously slow to make policy changes. Leo, who is considered a deliberative decision maker, is unlikely to speed up that process, according to Véronique Lecaros, a professor of theology at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru.

“I think he’s very sensitive to the topic,” said Ms. Lecaros, the president of a commission that collected testimony from abuse victims in Lima. But, she added, “he’s not somebody to hurry up.”

Camila Bustamante, one of the survivors who met with the pope, said she expected the Church to have made more progress in financial reparations to victims.

But she remains hopeful, she said, that Leo will eventually act. “He’s been in for a very short amount of time,” she said.

Lucía Cholakian Herrera contributed reporting from Buenos Aires.
